items.title: Elisa Longo Borghini wins eighth Italian time trial title in Piasco
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Elisa Longo Borghini wrapped up her season by claiming her eighth Italian individual time trial title in Piasco, following the postponement of the event originally scheduled for June. The UAE Team ADQ rider reclaimed the jersey after finishing runner-up to Vittoria Guazzini (FDJ United-Suez) in each of the past two years. Longo Borghini previously won the title in 2014, 2016, 2017, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023.

The 34-year-old rider averaged 50.839 km/h on the 19.7km flat and fast course, stopping the clock with a time of 23:15. Alessia Vigilia (Uno-X Mobility) took second, 54 seconds in arrears, while Letizia Borghesi (AG Insurance-Soudal) rounded out the podium.

The out-and-back route with 102 metres of climbing headed towards Costigliole Saluzzo before tackling two laps of a 6.7km circuit.

“I’m very happy to have won another Italian National Championship because I believe it’s a race that should always be honoured, even though this year it came at the end of a very long season," Longo Borghini said in a team release.

"It was a title I really wanted, because wearing the Italian champion’s jersey is always an honour. I’ll be happy to wear it next year in some of the biggest races on the WorldTour calendar."

The U23 title went to Giada Silo (UAE Development Team), who also claimed the Italian Road Race title in the Under-23 category back in June.

The Italian Cycling Federation postponed the junior, U23 and elite women’s time trial championships until late October, relocating the races to Piasco. The new date and location in the province of Cuneo were announced on October 8. The elite men’s event, won by Filippo Ganna (Netcompany Ineos), had gone ahead as scheduled in June in Barolo.

Guazzini did not defend her title, with just five riders lining up for the elite women’s time trial, down sharply from the 21 who contested last year’s event in June.

This season, Longo Borghini finished fourth in the ITT at both the World Championships and European Championships, and helped Italy win gold in the mixed relay at the Worlds. She also soloed to her seventh Italian road race title in June before finishing third at Tour de France Femmes and taking bronze in the road race at the World Championships.

items.title: HG Cross Heerderstrand: Joran Wyseure outpowers Joris Nieuwenhuis to claim first win of the season
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Joran Wyseure (Crelan-Corendon) claimed his first win of the cyclo-cross season on the lake-side course at the HG Cross Heerderstrand in the Netherlands.

In a final-lap duel with defending champion Joris Nieuwenhuis (Heizomat-Cube), the Belgian used his power to full effect in the sand section, taking the longer line close to the water to find traction on the wet sand. The move gave him a few seconds of breathing room, which he steadily extended to seven seconds by the finish line.

Defending champion Niels Vandeputte (Alpecin-Premier Tech) took third, crossing the line, 16 seconds later ahead of Felipe Orts and 18-year-old Giel Lejeune (Alpecin-Premier Tech).

“It means a lot for me. I think every win is special, and it's a nice circuit here. I think it was a nice battle also with Joran and Niels, and I'm really happy I could make it off,” Wyseure said.

As the light changed quickly from red to green, riders on the left-hand side, including Wyseure, Orts, Laurens Sweeck (Crelan-Corendon) and Pim Ronhaart (Baloise Verzekeringer-Het Poetsbureau Lions), seemed not to be paying attention and had a slow start, and only Wyseure and Orts were able to recover to make it to the front of the race.

In the opening rounds of the nine-lap race. The front of the race shuffled and re-shuffled until six riders escaped at the end of the fourth lap, with Nieuwenhuis, Vandeputte, Orts, Mees Hendrikx (Bomba-Join), Lejeune and Wyseure making the front group.

With the sunny and slightly windy conditions drying out the course, riders were taking and testing the two different lines on the deep sand sections, with a shorter inside line and the more compacted sand on the outside, longer line.

At the end of the seventh lap, Wyseure powered to the front and applied pressure, with Hendrixx falling off the pace. He stayed at the front for the next lap, stretching out the group with his high pace until the elastic broke.

With one lap to go, Wyseure and Nieuwenhuis were locked in a duel until Wyseure broke away, giving a final look over his shoulder before speeding down the finishing straight.

items.title: HG Cross Heerderstrand: Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado delivers assured ride to triumph in elite women's race
items.author: Katy Madgwick
items.content:
Dutch national champion Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado (Fenix-Premier Tech) scored her first victory of the fledgling 2026-2027 cyclo-cross season with a patient yet dominant display on the banks of the Heerderstrand in the Netherlands this Saturday.

A powerful attack on the final lap saw the former world champion distance Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen) and Manon Bakker, after the three battled for supremacy throughout the second half of the race. A spirited comeback from Aniek van Alphen saw the 777TV rider take third place behind Betsema after she caught and passed Bakker in the final straight.

Prior to the race, it was the official launch of Fem van Empel's new team, Specialized TMRW, that took centre stage, following van Empel's return to the field last weekend in Meulebeke. The former world champion immediately imposed herself on the race, taking the lead within the first minute of racing, with Leonie Bentveld (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez-Industriebouw) hot on her heels.

The two leading riders took two very different approaches on the long sand section, with van Empel dismounting and running close to the barriers, while Bentveld stayed on her bike and rode along the lakefront. It wasn't enough to separate them, but van Empel appeared to be in ominous form, carving out a small gap as lap 1 wore on, but by the time they crossed the finish line for the first time, a group of five riders had joined her, with 777TV’s Hélène Clauzel taking up the front position heading into lap 2. The group stayed together through the first part of the second lap, but Betsema rode aggressively, striking out into the lead and opening up a gap to the chase group, with Clauzel taking the initiative and leading the chase.

Betsema’s lead continued to grow heading into the third lap of six, and she continued her dogged progress, with the shape of the chase group changing behind her. Alvarado and Bakker were the two riders who eventually clawed Betsema back to form a leading trio on lap 4, with Van Alphen in solo pursuit in fourth, and both Van Empel and Clauzel fading.

Alvarado's strength through the sand section may have struck an ominous warning on lap 4, with Betsema briefly faltering in her wake, but a mistake for the Dutch champion as her foot slipped out meant that they were all back together as a trio again heading into lap 5.

They remained that way until Bakker began to exert her authority, using her power to begin to test Betsema, who was the first to lose touch, struggling to hang onto the lead pair under the continued pressure by the bullish Bakker, who was opening her European season following 6 victories from 8 races in the USA.

Heading into the final lap, however, Betsema dug deep to bring herself back into contention, and with the podium finishers all but decided it was down to the three riders who had proven they were strongest on the day to battle it out to decide their finishing positions. Bakker appeared to pay for her big effort on lap 5 as she began to slip away on the final lap, and Alvarado powered her way into the final long sand section, controlling her bike well and then running confidently to stretch out her lead over the pair of chasers.

It was a decisive strike by Alvarado, with both Bakker and Betsema fading on the final lap while behind them, van Alphen enjoyed a spirited late surge to throw her hat in the ring for a podium spot. Her dogged pursuit paid off, as she closed down Bakker in the final section of the course to set up a two-up sprint for second with Betsema. Her efforts proved costly, however, with Betsema able to hold her off to seal second spot.

items.title: Tom Pidcock finishes career-best fifth in UCI rankings with Pinarello Q36.5 bringing in major reinforcements for 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Tom Pidcock closed out the 2026 season with a career-best fifth in the UCI rankings, leading Pinarello Q36.5 to their best season yet as they punched well above their weight as a ProTeam to finish as the 12th-best team in the world.

Out-ranking six of the 18 WorldTour teams, the Swiss team won nine races, including Eddie Dunbar's stunning stage victory at the Vuelta a España, and five for Pidcock, including Milano-Torino, and a stage of the Tour of the Alps.

With top-10 results also at Strade Bianche, Il Lombardia, GP de Quebec, GP de Montreal, Tour of Guangxi, and the World Championships road race, Pidcock scored fewer UCI points than Pogačar, Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), and Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM).

"Tom finishing fifth in the world, the highest ranking of his career, is another exceptional milestone," said Team Principal Doug Ryder on Pinarello Q36.5's website.

"He is one of the most talented athletes in cycling, and his achievements reflect both his extraordinary ability and the environment we are building around our riders to help them perform at their very best."

At 27, Pidcock will lead Pinarello Q36.5 for the third year running in 2027, with major reinforcements in the form of Giulio Ciccone, Mauro Schmid, Ethan Hayter, and AJ August, to name just four of their 10 new signings.

They'll be looking to build on the foundations of these past 10 months and four seasons of major growth since they became Q36.5, with Ryder crediting the culture of innovation and responsibility as factors in their success.

"Finishing 12th in the world is an outstanding achievement and a defining moment for our organisation. We are a UCI ProTeam competing against the very best teams in professional cycling, and this result demonstrates the strength of our vision, the quality of our people and the progress we have made together," said Ryder.

"What makes me particularly proud is that this achievement reflects the commitment, professionalism and belief of every rider, every member of staff and every partner who contributes to this project. We have built a culture where ambition is matched by hard work, where innovation drives performance and where every individual understands their responsibility towards our collective success.

"I also want to recognise our owners and partners, whose commitment and confidence in this project have been fundamental to our development. Their support allows us to think differently, invest in the right people and continue challenging the established order of professional cycling."

Pidcock scored more than four times more UCI points than Quinten Hermans – the next highest scorer on Pinarello Q36.5 – a similar multiplier to how much he outscored his next best teammate in 2025. With Schmid and Ciccone especially, the Brit has other big-name riders entering the equation as potential leaders at one-day races and at the Grand Tours, taking some of the pressure off his shoulders and likely ensuring he has more support in the finales of the biggest races.

items.title: 'An alien like Tadej Pogačar might be able to do it' – Red Bull boss Denk would prefer Remco Evenepoel doesn't do Giro d'Italia-Tour de France double in 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
While Remco Evenepoel didn't rule out a return to the Giro d'Italia in 2027 before racing at Il Lombardia, the announcement of the Tour de France route has seen his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk admit he's against his star rider doing the double.

Racing at the Giro would mark his first return to the Italian Grand Tour since COVID-19 forced him out of the 2023 edition, having just taken the lead in the race before the first rest day. Speaking before the final Monument of the season, Evenepoel said: "The door is open," though he did immediately assure that was by no means a guarantee: "But that doesn't mean I'll start, mind you!"

The announcement of the Tour's route last Thursday and confirmation of a double individual time trial, and the most ITT kilometres since the 2012 edition – where specialist Bradley Wiggins took victory – have made that seem less likely. He was second behind only Tadej Pogačar at the Tour this past season, so anything but a return would be a surprise, especially with perhaps the best-suited route to his characteristics in years.

Asked whether the Giro-Tour double could be on the cards for Evenepoel in 2027, Denk admitted: "Here too, it is way too early to make a decision, but personally, I am not a fan of it. An alien like Tadej Pogačar might be able to do it, but…" speaking to at the presentation in Paris on Thursday.

So does Denk not put his rider in the same 'Alien' category? – asked the Belgian publication – "Let’s just say there have been enough examples of ‘ trial and error’ in the past. It seems better to me to focus on one of the two. But anyway, I’m not a sports scientist who can provide you with super-accurate information on this. We’ll see.

"The big advantage of our project is that we have a wide range of potential Grand Tour leaders at our disposal. We also have Florian Lipowitz, Jai Hindley, and some young, fast-developing talents like Giulio Pellizzari and Lorenzo Finn. There isn’t just Remco. Definitely, without a doubt.”

Rumours for the Giro's route in 2027 are not as concrete as those preceding the Tour route's confirmation, but there is talk of two time trials potentially also featuring in Italy – but one is expected to be a mountain time trial from Sulmona-Campo di Giove. Also running against Evenepoel's advantage is the expectation of a much harder climbing route than that of the Tour, which only features three summit finishes.

The 2027 Giro d'Italia route will be revealed on November 3, but it won't be until December 11 that Red Bull confirm the 2027 programme of Evenepoel. Anything but the Tour de France being the focus of his summer looks set to be a major surprise, so RCS and the Giro may have to wait another year until he potentially returns to the pink race.

items.title: 'The only way to beat Pogačar is through time trial kilometres' - Tom Dumoulin backs Remco Evenepoel at 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Katy Madgwick
items.content:
Speaking to , Dumoulin outlined his reaction to the 2027 route after organisers ASO officially presented it in Paris on Thursday. "I personally think it’s great that they’re starting in Great Britain. I started there myself back in 2014,” he said of the 2027 Grand Départ.

“It was absolutely brilliant – an incredible experience. So, it’s wonderful that they’re heading back there. But, of course, that was already known. What hadn’t been revealed yet was that this Tour includes a massive number of time-trial kilometres. That is, without a doubt, the most striking feature of this route, especially considering the trend we’ve seen in recent years, where Grand Tour courses have featured very few time-trial kilometres."

The former Visma-Lease a Bike rider, who won the 2017 World Championships in the discipline, would undoubtedly have benefited from such a course during his time competing at the Tour, between 2013 and 2020. His debut participation in 2013 featured the longest distance raced against the clock (90km) prior to next year's 71km, across three time trials - one team time trial and two individual efforts. He finished in second place in 2018, behind overall winner Geraint Thomas, in a year with 66.5km of time trials.

Dumoulin, along with Remco Evenepoel and other specialists, may feel as if they are children of a bygone era, as historically, the Tour has featured far more in the way of time trial kilometres, not just in its early years, but all the way through to the 1980s and even early 2000s.

The modern trend away from long time trials arguably began in 2008, the first year to feature less than 100 kilometres against the clock since 1975. In fact, the last time there were more than 100 kilometres of time trials within one edition was in 2012, the year before Dumoulin made his Tour debut - all of them individual time trials, making that the last year to feature more ITT kilometres than 2027.

In 2027, the longest ITT stage - stage 7 from Blois to Chambord - still only clocks in at 38km, with a second time trial around Toulouse on stage 16 coming in at a marginally shorter 33km; but with a total of 71 kilometres against the clock, it’s the most friendly parcours to the ITT specialists since 2013.

Dumoulin doesn’t underestimate the significance of this shift to Evenepoel.

"Now, they’ve completely changed course, with roughly 70 kilometres of individual time trials in total. That certainly gets my heart racing - and I imagine it does the same for Remco Evenepoel," Dumoulin said.

He goes on to suggest that despite a lack of summit finishes, it may actually produce a more exciting race overall, particularly in the face of the daunting challenge presented by five-time winner Tadej Pogačar and his all-conquering UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad.

"In the last Tour, the outcome was effectively decided quite early on,” Dumoulin said. “I think the Tour organisers are clearly keen to find some way to keep the dominance of UAE and Pogačar in check. By designing a route that keeps things competitive until quite late in the Tour. The only way to beat Pogačar is through time trial kilometres."

items.title: Who will win the 2027 Tour de France? The favourites for the yellow jersey following the route reveal
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The 2027 Tour de France route was presented on Thursday, and the race looks markedly different from the 2026 parcours, with an increase in time trial kilometres and fewer big mountain stages lying between the British Grand Départ and the grand finale in Paris.

Nevertheless, we expect a familiar cast of contenders to line up in Edinburgh on July 2, including the five-time champion Tadej Pogačar, his longtime rival, Jonas Vingegaard, and France's great GC hope, Paul Seixas.

We're a long way from the start of the action, and most of the big Tour contenders haven't turned a wheel in anger in a while, but which riders are shaping up as the main favourites at this early stage?

We've looked through the big names to put together our first speculative 'power ranking' ahead of the 2027 Tour de France.

But unlike Prudhomme, who has a vested interest in generating attention for his race, we have no reason to doubt that the Slovenian will recover and be back to his best next season.

As such, Pogačar remains the overwhelming favourite to win Tour title number six next July. The route may feature an increase in time trial kilometres, which will favour the next man on our list, but Pogačar has won the last three Tours by an average of 5:42.

We're hoping that the new route means there's more suspense than this summer, when the race for yellow was over after six days. But Pogačar is the favourite until proven otherwise.

World and European time trial champion Remco Evenepoel looks to be the big winner from the 2027 Tour de France route reveal. 71 time trial kilometres is the most on any Tour route since 2012, and 12km more than the 2024 Tour.

That, combined with the sparse number of tough summit finishes (just two – the Grand Colombier and Col du Portet), means the route is the best-suited to Evenepoel's abilities of any Grand Tour he's raced.

There has been talk of Evenepoel returning to the Giro d'Italia next May, but surely he won't turn down the chance to take on a Tour so well-suited to his style?

Two-time Tour winner Jonas Vingegaard looks to be the biggest loser from the route reveal, with the 2027 parcours very much veering away from his favoured terrain. The Dane prefers longer multi-mountain stages, days which are in short supply here, and then there are the two flat time trials which will hardly have sparked any excitement when they were unveiled on Thursday.

A host of punchier and mid-mountain stages such as those to Le Creusot, Sallanches, Les Saisies, and Mende all favour the more explosive Pogačar. Both the Slovenian and Remco Evenepoel will gain time on Vingegaard in the 71km of time trials, too (remember in Caen at the 2025 Tour, where he lost over a minute to both in just 33km).

Could Vingegaard make up the time lost in the time trials in the mountains, on the Grand Colombier and the Col du Portet? That's likely several minutes to make up on Evenepoel across those combined 33.4km of summit finishes.

The 2027 Tour de France route isn't exactly built for France's new GC hope Paul Seixas, though he won't necessarily dislike it. Sure, there aren't many mountain stages for him to attack, but that's true of everyone else here.

The 20-year-old showed in his debut Tour de France this year that he's already strong enough to battle with the very biggest names, even if he's not quite on the level of Pogačar, Evenepoel, Vingegaard, and Isaac del Toro just yet. Next year, though? He should be stronger still.

He's proven that he's strong in the mountains, he can compete with the best in the punchy hills, and (see his third place in the Worlds time trial) that he's very capable in flat time trials, even if he should shed a chunk of time to Evenepoel in them.

For now, we'll slot him in fourth place on our list, assuming some level of progression year on year, and with Del Toro working for Pogačar. Could a podium place be in his sights, though?

Mexican racer Isaac del Toro finished in third place last year in the white jersey of best young rider while supporting Tadej Pogačar to yet another Tour victory. He was the Slovenian's key lieutenant while also benefiting from his support to ride into that eventual podium spot.

Will they reform the same partnership next summer? Or will Del Toro instead prioritise going for a Grand Tour victory of his own at the Giro or Vuelta?

That remains to be seen, with the calendars of him and João Almeida yet to be determined. If he's back at the Tour, then Del Toro should slot back in somewhere among the third- to fifth- strongest GC riders on the startlist.

Will Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe continue with their two-pronged leadership approach at next year's Tour de France? Maybe not, if some media rumours are to be believed. Given the route of next year's race, that might make sense, given it clearly favours time trial specialist Remco Evenepoel over German racer Florian Lipowitz.

Lipowitz is hardly a weak time triallist himself, and he has of course finished on the Tour's final podium before, but perhaps a shot at overall victory at the Giro d'Italia might be in order.

If Lipowitz does head to the Tour, though, he slots in well inside our top 10 here, even if there are fewer high mountain stages where he excels in comparison to previous years.

When Tadej Pogačar crashed out of the Vuelta a España in August, Movistar leader Enric Mas showed another dimension to his racing as he took over the red jersey of race leader and defended it for the final two weeks of the race to take overall victory.

Mas had previously finished on the podium of the Spanish Grand Tour four times in his career but had never managed to break through to that next level. Will his triumph, and the rare show of attacking riding we saw, have unlocked another level in the 31-year-old?

Mas has raced seven Tours de France, finishing fifth and sixth at the 2020 and 2021 races. In a crowded GC field, he might slot in around there again, with his Vuelta win and the confidence gained from that lifting him in our ranking above a host of other strong competitors.

Dane Mattias Skjelmose might head to the Tour de France as part of a three-pronged GC lineup at Lidl-Trek next year, though surely one of him, Felix Gall, and Juan Ayuso will instead prioritise the Giro d'Italia.

Regardless of the German team's plans for the 2027 Grand Tours, it's he who figures to be their strongest option for Tour de France leadership next summer. He finished sixth overall in July, and had the better of Ayuso, who seemed to struggle this season, while Gall's lack of time trial strength will surely hold him back.

Skjelmose is the best of the three against the clock, as evidenced by his third place in Thonon-les-Bains at the Tour. Barring any surprise, he looks the favourite to be Lidl-Trek leader next July. Can he raise his level again and challenge for the podium? It seems a bit of a reach right now, but contention for a top-five place could be on the cards.

The last time the Tour de France had this many time trial kilometres, Netcompany Ineos were certainly a very different team. Back then, in 2021, Bradley Wiggins raced to overall victory. This time around, the odds are stacked against the British squad, and even a podium spot would be a miracle result.

The team has a few options for leadership next July, including Oscar Onley (more below), and Carlos Rodríguez, should the Spaniard rediscover his form. The best option, given the route, may well be Dutch rider Thymen Arensman.

Should he head to the Tour, Arensman would line up as one of the very strongest time trial riders among the GC contenders, and the 71km of TTs on offer represent significant time gains. He has four Grand Tour top-10 finishes to his name, including a fourth at this year's Giro, and took 12th at the 2025 Tour. He'd be more than capable of scoring a top 10 in Paris, given next year's route.

Like several others on our list, we'll have to wait and see what Felix Gall is planning for 2027. The Austrian climber will be on a new team next year, having swapped Decathlon CMA CGM for Lidl-Trek and a potential leadership trio at the Tour.

Surely one of the three - Skjelmose, Gall, and Juan Ayuso – will instead head to the Giro as a sole leader, though. It depends on the Italian race's route, but could it be Gall? After all, two long time trials are hardly his forte (though the Giro also looks set to feature heavy time trial kilometres).

Gall is a rider who is at his best in the high mountains, tackling long ascents on multi-mountain stages. As we have seen, they are in short supply in this Tour de France. There's still plenty of opportunity to gain time in the climbs, but the route isn't best-suited to Gall.

Reigning mountain classification champion Richard Carapaz will be with a new team next year, having joined NSN. The team doesn't have a great record of hiring big-name riders in their 30s, but there's little in the Ecuadorian's riding style that suggests he's heading there to ride around cashing cheques.

While Thymen Arensman may be better suited to the route, Netcompany Ineos also has Oscar Onley – a fourth-place finisher here in 2025 – on board as a Tour co-leadership option. A repeat of that result looks challenging, but both he and Arensman should be well in the mix for a top-10 finish.

As noted earlier, Juan Ayuso currently looks the third-strongest of Lidl-Trek's GC options at the Tour. His new team expected more than seventh place out of him, and perhaps he'll do that in 2027. For now, though, he has slid down our list.

A year on from his Vuelta podium, Tom Pidcock raced to ninth overall this summer. It was his best result to date at the Tour, but will he continue to target the general classification?

Both Tobias Halland Johanessen and Lenny Martinez have raced into the top 10 in the past two seasons. Neither are top favourites for a high placing next summer, but they've been there and done that, and so should be in consideration for a top-10 spot again.

items.title: EF Education-EasyPost sign Worlds medalist from Netcompany Ineos devo team, bring on Herzog from Red Bull
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
At just 22, Herzog has already raced at the top tier the last three seasons with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, taking a top 10 at Milano-Torino and Bretagne Classic-CIC. He nearly pulled off his first UCI victory on stage 5 at this year's Volta a la Comunitat Valenciana, getting into the decisive breakaway and going second in a six-rider sprint.

“Emil is a huge talent. He was junior world champion and, at 22, already has three years of WorldTour racing in his legs,” EF Pro Cycling founder and CEO Jonathan Vaughters said.

“He was knocking on the door of his first professional win this season. I think he is going to flourish in the years ahead. He is an aggressive racer who really fits into our team’s style. We’re going to give him every opportunity to show his skills and strength.”

In 2021, the German won the junior time trial national title and finished second at the Course de la Paix. The next season, he won 12 races, including Course de la Paix, the junior road race national and world titles.

Having grown up in the foothills of the Bavarian Alps, his passion for mountain biking and nordic skiing led him to try Unbound Gravel 200 in Kansas, where he surprised with eighth in the elite field. On the road, he sees himself developing as a climber, and looks for opportunities to be aggressive to forge his way to the front in one-day and stage races where he overcomes fatigue for a final kick.

"In the juniors, I was more of a sprinter, a bit more of a classics rider, but I've turned a bit more into a climber type," he said in a press release.

"But my goal should be to get back that explosiveness, because I love going in breakaways, and if I'm in a group that comes to the finish, I'd love to be able to win the sprint out of it. My fatigue resistance is quite good, so it's good for me when we have to push the whole day."

Milesi moves up to the WorldTour for the first time after a year with Netcompany Ineos Racing Academy. He began his career as a junior mountain bike champion then switched to the road, where he earned three consecutive silver medals in the U23 Italian time trial championships.

At Montréal Road Worlds, he was just seven seconds off the winning pace in the U23 time trial, won by Dutch rider Ryan Gal. But three weeks later he concluded his year with a victory in the U23 Chrono des Nations. He also won a time trial stage at Olympia's Tour. Showing the versatility that attracted EF Education, the Italian won the 164.5km Gran Premio Sportivi di Poggiana one-day race using his fast kick at the end to win a two-up sprint from a breakaway.

“In the summer, I started talking to EF Education-EasyPost, and what was clear was that this team was an excellent opportunity for my progression and development as a rider. I wanted to step up and join the WorldTour, and I’m really happy with my decision for the next few years,” Nicolas said in a team press release.

Herzog and Milesi are both signed through 2029, while Bayer has a two-year contract.

Bayer has proven his versatility during six years at Alpecin-Premier Tech, from a domestique role in six Grand Tours to finishing on the podium at Brussels Cycling Classic. A former two-time Austrian U23 time trial national champion, the 26-year-old seeks opportunities in breakaways and relishes the aggressive style of EF Education-EasyPost.

"He’s shown that he is an incredibly devoted teammate who won’t hesitate to turn himself inside out for the cause. That said, we think he still has untapped potential and we are excited to see what he can do,” Vaughters said.

items.title: 'I will retire soon' – Marlen Reusser discusses future as she gives thumbs up to Paula Blasi's arrival at Movistar in 2027
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Marlen Reusser has given her strongest hint yet that her racing days may soon be numbered when the Swiss time trialling star was asked at the Tour de France Femmes presentation about the imminent arrival of Spanish up-and-coming racer Paula Blasi at her Movistar squad.

Blasi had a breakthrough season in 2026 while racing for UAE Team L'IMAD, winning La Vuelta Femenina and Amstel Gold Race, before taking fifth at her debut Tour de France Femmes.

Reusser also had a highly successful Tour, winning the mid-race TT and holding the lead for three days before losing the yellow jersey on Mont Ventoux, before dropping to 14th overall after crashing on the final day in Nice.

Speaking at the Tour de France Femmes route presentation, Reusser also said that it was a pity there was no individual time trial in 2027 but praised the inclusion of the team time trial on stage 3 in London and the Ardennes-like stages 2 and 8.

Whilst pointing out that the Tour is often decided, at least in part, on less mountainous stages, she also said that she was confident of her chances of handling the critical Puy de Dôme climb and its ultra-steep finale.

"I think the Puy de Dôme is closed off to riders right now" – the road is usually shut because the entire volcano is an ecologically sensitive site – "but I remember watching the Tour go up it in 2023; it's a cool climb to finish the Tour," Reusser said.

"I think I can manage the slopes [of 12%] well. I have no idea if it's possible to recon, but if so I'll do it."

Regarding the absence of an individual time trial, reigning world and European champion Reusser confirmed she would have liked that "because that does something very different with the GC. It's not the same. But in any case I love the discipline [of team time trialling], and I think that's very cool."

The very hilly stages could, in any case, be as important for the GC as the setpiece mountain days, of which there is really only the last, as Reusser pointed out, to the point where they might actually decide the race overall. Stage 4 of last year's Tour was a good example of this, where it played a major part in sorting out the GC, with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot showing significant signs of weakness that day.

"Sometimes it's like this, we look at the big mountain stages, but often these [hilly] stages are actually the more important," Reusser said.

"I was just asked if next year's Tour is not as hard as this year. Ok, the big mountains are there, they sound hard, but these hilly stages are even harder in a way, so they can be very crucial for the GC. We saw it last year."

As for whether there would be another 'Project Dijon' for Reusser, similar to the one she built around the time trial last July in the Tour de France Femmes, Reusser smiled but said it was too early to target specific stages.

"I am sure my DS is waiting in the back there; we'll make plans, we have a lot of time to think about what we're going to do with this race, and we'll have some projects for sure," she said..

The question of how long Reusser will continue racing, though, emerged when she was asked how she felt about the arrival of Blasi on the team. Under contract until the end of 2027, Reusser said that she would retire "soon" and pointed out that at 35, she was no longer as young as she once was.

Reusser also said that having a rider like Blasi on the squad offered Movistar an excellent opportunity to plan for a double assault on the Tour GC, given the Spaniard's proven ability to attack in hilly terrain as she did to win Amstel Gold Race last year.

"For Paula, I think this Tour route is perfect because when you see the Ardennes-like stages, I think it's good to have good riders because you can make good tactics," she reasoned.

"And I think she will want to win the Tour in the future, and I think that's a nice thing. I will retire soon. I'm not the youngest anymore, so I think it makes sense to have her on the team; she's a very big talent. It is the Spanish team, too, so that's nice."

Reusser's career has seen her take multiple top time trial titles, including the World Championships as well as holding the leader's jersey in the Tour last summer.

But if she is now thinking that she may be hanging up her wheels in the shorter rather than the longer term, whilst clearly with plans to shine next summer in the Tour again, then Blasi may well be the ideal way for Movistar to keep battling for Grand Tours in the future.

items.title: Fem van Empel leads Specialized TMRW cyclo-cross team set to 'open new pathways for the next generation' of road talent
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The Specialized TMRW cycling project is now official, as FDJ United-SUEZ and Specialized confirmed Friday the roster and plans for a new multi-disciplinary approach for a long-term progression to develop talent on the road.

Four core riders will comprise the squad for the 2026-2027 cyclo-cross season, led by three-time cyclo-cross world champion Fem van Empel, who has already provided a sneak preview of the red team kits with her fourth-place finish last weekend at Berencross in Meulebeke, Belgium.

She'll be joined for off-road racing by Anja Grossmann, Amandine Muller and Célia Gery, the trio all U23 riders on the road with FDJ United-SUEZ. Last year, Gery earned the women's U23 bronze medal at Cyclo-cross World Championships in Hulst, while Muller was fifth, both racing for France. Grossman, an 18-year-old talent from Switzerland, went fourth in the women's junior race at CX Worlds last season.

The TMRW brand was created by Tomorrow Group, the owner of FDJ United-SUEZ, to broaden racing into new disciplines. Cyclo-cross was noted as the first step in "strengthening its international presence and nurturing outstanding young talent" as the discipline was seen as a way for riders to develop technical skills and earn racing experience throughout the year.

Stephen Delcourt, the general manager for the Women's WorldTour squad, will serve in the same capacity for the French cyclo-cross team, with Nicolas Maire serving dual roles as well as the sports director.

“What we are building today is rooted in the project developed with FDJ UNITED and SUEZ. Their commitment allows us to look further ahead and prepare for the next stages of our development. Together with Specialized, we share the conviction that giving young athletes the opportunity to grow across disciplines can help them become more complete road riders," Del Court said in a team statement.

"Specialized TMRW brings that ambition to life: to open new pathways for the next generation, explore new sporting opportunities and continue expanding internationally.

"Cyclo-cross has played an important role in the development of some of cycling’s greatest athletes. It provides a demanding environment in which to build technical skills, confidence and racing instinct. We want to give our riders who share that passion the best possible conditions to develop and perform, in full alignment with their goals on the road."

The creation of Specialized TMRW aligns with the road team’s 2030 strategic plan, which management said strived for "excellence in both disciplines".

Van Empel joined FDJ United-SUEZ in mid-September, having taken nearly a year off from racing and securing a release from her multi-year contract with Visma-Lease a Bike. She won a bronze medal in the women's junior road race at European Road Championships in 2023, then impressed the next year on the WorldTour stage with 11th overall at Giro d'Italia and a stage win and points classification title at Tour de l'Avenir Femmes.

Gery, the reigning French elite women's road national champion, won De Brabantse Pijl and a stage at the Giro d'Italia this past season. A dual road and time trial junior champion of Switzerland for two consecutive years, Grossmann impressed at the Road World Championships with fourth in the ITT and a bronze medal in the road race.

Muller, who just turned 20 in mid-October, raced for the AG Insurance Soudal development team the past two seasons, winning the French U23 time trial title twice and the women's elite ITT at the Mediterranean Games.

The Dutch rider's new contract for CX and road goes through 2027, while Gery and Grossman are signed through 2028, Muller through 2029.

"Specialized TMRW builds on the long-term project developed with FDJ UNITED SUEZ, whose commitment remains central to the team’s development," management of the new team said in a statement.

In addition to support from Specialized for the cyclo-cross campaign, the project was also supported by 100%, Shimano and Gobik.

items.title: Why breaking contracts continues to become more common in cycling – Pogačar's agent Carera offers explanation after early exits of Ganna, Carapaz, and Ciccone
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
In previous eras of cycling, a rider breaking their contract early to move teams could have caused major controversy, but in the past few weeks, big-name riders Richard Carapaz, Filippo Ganna, and Giulio Ciccone have all announced exits before the end to join new teams without any obvious hitches.

As riders leaving their current teams early for new pastures becomes more common in the peloton – a practice not just isolated to the men's pros either, with Paula Blasi doing the same – it marks a transformation of the transfer market, with almost any rider available, in theory.

Ciccone's agent Alex Carera, whose agency A&J All Sports also represents Blasi, and a certain Tadej Pogačar, spoke to to explain some of the reasons why this is happening more and more.

"First of all, the average length of contracts has increased - by a lot. Therefore, the likelihood of arguments over a long contract, and even termination, increases," said Carera.

"In essence, if the contract is only two years long and problems arise, you shouldn't wait that long for it to expire, and it's not even worth arguing about. You might sulk for a year, and then you move on. But if, for example, the contract is five years long, it's easy to see that things are very different."

In recent years, several of the biggest riders in the world have reached agreements to leave their teams early: Remco Evenepoel and Primož Roglič both to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Juan Ayuso to Lidl-Trek, for example, and Carera says this is down partly to changes in team ownership.

"The second reason is even more crucial, considering that if you want to break an existing contract, you don't just have to negotiate with one team, but also have another team ready to sign you," added Carera.

"Here's the thing: until 5-6 years ago, in most cases the team owners were the team managers, often former cyclists. They didn't have a long-term vision, and they didn't risk potential penalties for signing riders from other teams.

"[Some of the] team owners are... the sponsors themselves. UAE, Decathlon, Lidl, Red Bull, to name a few. They have a more managerial, long-term vision. The cycling team is a key asset for the company, or the fund, unlike before, where there was often no entrepreneurial vision.

"And there's a greater tendency to be more 'aggressive' on the market, because they have to value the annual investment in cycling. Not to mention the fact that the capital invested is much greater. A momentous change."

The UCI overhauled the rules on how riders under contract with one WorldTour can enter into discussions and start the process of joining another. To prevent controversial poaching and the type of polemic that unfolded around the early departure of Cian Uijtdebroeks – another one of Carera's riders – from Visma to Red Bull, the UCI introduced the requirement for a three-party agreement between the rider, their current team, and the new team to enact the move.

Asked what the turning point was for the new types of transfers that were once very rare becoming more and more common by the season, Carera specifically pointed to the transfer of the Belgian, and the financial growth in the sport that followed.

"Cian Uijtdebroeks' early departure from Bora to join Visma in December 2023, a move that generated significant media attention and involved two top teams," he said.

"Until then, early contract terminations occurred once every three years; now, they're about 10 a year. And then, capital has increased enormously: in 2020, if a team had a budget of €25 million, it could be considered wealthy. Now, it would be in the bottom five."

There was one rider whose lengthy ongoing deal is an exception to the new freedom for aggression in the transfer market: Pogačar, whose 2032 contract puts him as one of the most tied-down riders to their ongoing deal, alongside those who have 'lifetime' contracts until retirement: Wout van Aert, Marianne Vos, and Mads Pedersen.

"Is Tadej Pogacar the exception?" asked Ciro Scognamiglio. "Yes, because it has too high a value, the clause is almost symbolic: Tadej has gone beyond the boundaries of cycling," replied Carera.

items.title: Could 71km of time trialing actually help Remco Evenepoel win the Tour de France? A closer look at exactly what the Belgian could gain against Pogačar
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Not since Bradley Wiggins won the 2012 Tour de France have there been as many individual time trial kilometres on the route of cycling's biggest race, with the 71km included on the 2027 route swinging the balance towards the best ITT rider in the peloton and four-time World Champion Remco Evenepoel.

While no route can really be anti-Tadej Pogačar, this is about as good as it can get for the Belgian, with only three summit finishes and almost all of the hardest climbs being backloaded in the second two thirds of the route. Runner-up in 2026 to the Slovenian, Evenepoel will surely be back at the Tour in July, with his eye on at least a repeat GC performance.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk didn't go over the top with his assessment of the route and the advantages Evenepoel might seek to gain, but it is clear that a more TT-heavy Grand Tour will always suit his attributes.

"A dream Tour profile for Remco Evenepoel? Hmm, I see that a little differently. More nuanced," he said to at the presentation in Paris, before conceding that, on paper at least, stages 7 and 16 being mostly flat races against the clock should play into their hands.

"In 2012, when Bradley Wiggins won, there were even more than 100. But anyway, it's not bad at all for us, let's say. Remco is currently the very best time trialist in the world, so that is an aspect of this Tour we are certainly going to take into account. That he can gain time on Pogačar, Vingegaard, Seixas and co. in those? In theory, yes."

"The multiple time trial kilometres will provide an extra dimension in any case and make the battle for the yellow jersey more open and exciting," said team Chief of Sports Zak Dempster in agreement.

But how much could the return to more than 70km of individual time trialling – for the first time in 14 years – really benefit Evenepoel in the fight against Pogačar?

Evenepoel only made his Tour debut in 2024, so the three editions he has taken on against the now five-time champion and joint record holder Pogačar have only brought them up against each other in five Grand Tour time trials.

All of those being at the Tour, the score for the moment is 3-2 in the favour of the Belgian, with Pogačar winning the two most climbing-packed stages against the clock in Nice at the end of the 2024 race, and on the pure mountain ITT to Peyragudes in 2025.

Evenepoel has beaten Pogačar to three stage wins at the flatter tests in Gevrey-Chambertin in 2024, Caen in 2025, and Thonon-les-Bains this past season, but the margin has never been major – 12 seconds, 16 seconds, and 28 seconds.

Yes, he has had the advantage – as he should on the completely flat stage 7 to Chambord and stage 16 in Toulouse, even with the viciously steep Côte de Pech David (800m at 12.%) characterising the middle of the route – but it's far from the complete domination that Evenepoel has subjected everyone, including Pogačar, to outside of the Grand Tours.

The image of Evenepoel riding past the usually immortal Slovenian's green jersey during the time trial at the World Championships in Kigali 13 months ago is one which will serve as a symbol of the Belgian's absolute monopoly over the discipline in recent memory, claiming the past four rainbow jerseys.

On that day, the monumental gap between their TT abilities wasn't only apparent in the overtake, but in the time difference at the finish: 2:37.

In fact, across their careers, they have faced off 12 times in individual time trials, Evenepoel winning 10 of them. Only on the two mountain courses at the Tour has he lost to Pogačar to against the clock.

So why does the gap seem to narrow significantly when they are racing in a time trial in the Tour?

The balance swinging massively in Pogačar's favour when an uphill road is included is no surprise – with less aerodynamic advantage for the 'Aero Bullet' Evenepoel at play, due to drag becoming less of a factor at slower speeds, and power-to-weight ratio (W/kg) becoming the more important variable.

But even on the flatter and purer courses, where Evenepoel has long been putting the likes of two-time World Champion Filippo Ganna to shame – most recently by a relatively huge 57 seconds at Worlds in Montreal, Pogačar is much closer during the Tour.

The likely answer comes down to weight, with Evenepoel admitting just this year that he arrived at the Tour almost 4kg down on the weight he had been operating at during the Classics. It's no secret that Evenepoel was in incredible condition for this year's Tour, putting up some of his best climbing performances with victory atop Plateau de Solaison, second on Alpe d'Huez, and keeping up with Pogačar for much longer in the second and third weeks than he has in previous years.

For events like the Worlds TT, where he destroyed Pogačar in Kigali as mentioned, Evenepoel operates at a higher weight, gaining around 1-2kg and losing some of his power-to-weight ratio as he ups the raw power numbers for his favoured discipline.

There's also the factor that no one in the peloton can maintain their level over three weeks like six-time Grand Tour winner Pogačar, whose repeatability and powers of recovery make him the perfect rider to take on punchy finishes, mountain stages and time trials day after day at the Tour – and compete for the win on all of them.

The best benchmark we have for how much time Evenepoel gain across 71 kilometres of time trials is the 28-second deficit he opened up to Pogačar at this year's Tour, over a course of just 26.1km.

Based on their average speeds from that day, 48.85kph for Evenepoel and 47.751kph for Pogačar, a perfect world would see the Belgian cover the 71km 1:05 faster than his rival – not exactly world-beating, but a time trial, with corners, ups and downs, and several accelerations, is far from a perfect world.

Evenepoel's advantage could become greater the longer they have to race, given he has the best aero TT position in the peloton, especially with the 71km being split into a flatter 38km effort, where the Belgian's edge should be magnified as the kilometres tick by. But the steep hill on stage 16 also plays massively into the hands of Pogačar, even at just 800 metres in length, equalising the equation between the pair. ]

The clear conclusion is that Evenepoel cannot rely just on his strongest weapon to truly take down the current benchmark – he will have to beat him, or, at the bare minimum, match him in the high mountains to stay in striking distance for the stages he will almost definitely win.

One other factor that the Belgian newspaper put to Red Bull management is how the arrival of the first mountain stage on stage 9 could help Evenepoel, who really built into his climbing powers this past July after struggling in the opening week.

"That can indeed be an advantage," said Denk. "On the other hand: if you go all out for the general classification, and that is what we always want to do with this team, you also have to be alert in those first ten days and control the situation."

Of his eventual 6:26 deficit to Pogačar in Paris, Evenepoel lost almost three minutes of that on stage 6, the first real big mountain day to Gavarnie-Gèdre. Losing just over three minutes over the remaining 15 stages was a massive step up, and could also play into the hands of the ever-developing Belgian star in his second year with Red Bull, but he'll have to cling onto Pogačar's wheel on stages like the brutal 18th to Col du Portet in a way that only really Jonas Vingegaard has been able to do since 2020 if he wants any hope of yellow.

items.title: 'The race will be wide open' – With no long climbs and no individual time trial, does the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route suit home favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot?
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Two summers ago, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot soared to a historic home victory at the Tour de France Femmes, dominating the closing Alpine stages to deliver a first French Tour win in decades and the biggest win of her career.

She beat Demi Vollering by almost four minutes in Châtel, but this year the tables turned as Ferrand-Prévot endured a disastrous title defence, losing minutes in the Dijon time trial before falling out of contention in the Ardèche hills and conceding defeat on Mont Ventoux.

Clearly, a rider of Ferrand-Prévot's calibre is better than her early-August performance, and the Visma-Lease a Bike star will aim to bounce back next year. But is the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route one where she can thrive and take back the yellow jersey from Vollering?

Well, race director Marion Rousse delivered both good and bad news for the 34-year-old and her team in the Palais des Congrès in Paris on Thursday afternoon.

For a start, there's no individual time trial on next year's route. That will be music to Ferrand-Prévot's ears after she lost two minutes to Vollering and Marlen Reusser over just 21km on the road to Dijon in August.

Ferrand-Prévot was always expected to shed time against the clock, even as her team protested how much she had trained on the TT bike, so for a start, she's already looking at several minutes saved. Coming in place of an individual time trial, however, is a team test in the form of a flat 18km tour of central London.

Team time trials are rare in women's cycling, with next year's stage a first in Tour de France Femmes history. The other Grand Tours have featured a TTT in recent history, though, with the Giro featuring one in 2021 and the Vuelta doing so between 2022 and 2025.

Do Visma have the personnel to succeed in such a test? Time will tell, and it's impossible to make any predictions this far out, but in former time trial specialist Jos van Emden, they have a directeur sportif well-placed to guide them in London.

"The team time trial is a notable feature. It’s an event we haven't seen before in the Tour de France Femmes," Van Emden said after the route unveiling.

"I'm a fan of team time trials. We haven't raced many of them as a team, so it's difficult to make any immediate predictions about our collective strength or the course in London. You have to master every discipline if you want to win the Tour. This will be another new challenge.

"That decision shows that women's cycling is continuing to evolve and grow in importance. A team time trial is part of what makes the Tour the Tour, as it’s the biggest stage in cycling."

Is there enough climbing for PFP?

The goal will likely be to limit losses and keep Ferrand-Prévot close to her main yellow jersey rivals as the race hits France, with the opening two stages in the north of England unlikely to have produced much in the way of GC gaps.

On the mainland, it will all be about surviving the pitfalls of the sprint stages and then overcoming the tricky, punchy hills on the road to Magnanville on stage 5.

The big time differences, however, should be made in the final three days as the race reaches the Massif Central, though there are no long Alpine climbs on the menu here like the Madeleine, where Ferrand-Prévot built her 2025 Tour victory with that dominant solo ride.

Will that be a problem for the lightweight climber?

"The first thing that stands out to me is how different this Tour is from the editions in recent years. The high mountains are missing. That was certainly different in previous editions," Van Emden said.

Stage 7 features a closing climb to La Loge des Gardes (6.7km at 7.1%), while the mid-mountain stage 8 to Clermont-Ferrand features the Côte de Charade (6km at 5.9%) before a descent to the finish. The showpiece final stage concludes atop the Puy de Dôme, which measures 11.3km at an average gradient of 7.8%.

Van Emden said that the Tour is no easier than the recent editions, even if the Puy de Dôme stage doesn't quite measure up to the recent queen stages of the Glandon-Alpe d'Huez in 2024, the Madeleine last year, or the Ventoux in August.

"The longest climb in this Tour is 11km. That was different in recent years. But that doesn’t mean this will be an easier Tour," he said.

"Quite the opposite: the race will be wide open, and the general classification contenders will be fighting for every second in every stage.

"That’s a very special way to finish. In cycling, this climb may not be as well known as Mont Ventoux or the Col de la Madeleine, which featured in recent editions, but that’s also because it’s a protected natural area. I’m really looking forward to finishing atop the volcano."

As is the case for the men's race, there's clearly one standout favourite for next year's Tour de France Femmes – the defending champion. This Tour route certainly isn't built with Ferrand-Prévot in mind, but success isn't out of reach, and if she's back on form, next August could well host the Ferrand-Prévot vs Vollering battle we've been waiting for.

Between now and then, there's plenty of time for training, planning, and recon rides. The planning will get underway soon, said Van Emden.

"We’ll draw up our plans this winter. With Pauline, we have the 2025 Tour winner on our team, although she would normally be better suited to the longer climbs.

"But we have several cards to play. I think this route suits us very well. It’s going to be an explosive Tour."

items.title: 'It's a question of resetting the balance' – Tour de France boss namechecks Bradley Wiggins and Federico Bahamontes to explain major increase in time trialling on 2027 route
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme delved deep into the race's own history books to explain exactly why organisers have opted in 2027 to make the biggest increase in time trialling in the route in 15 years

Instead, Prudhomme cited time trialling star Bradley Wiggins, who conquered Britain's first Tour de France in 2012, and the rider voted the race's greatest ever climber, 1959 winner Federico Martín Bahamontes, to explain the TT increase.

Rather than looking back at just the last three editions of the race, where Tadej Pogačar has effectively made the battle for the yellow jersey a one-man show, Prudhomme used a much bigger context to explain what provides the chance – though it's far from guaranteed – for a radical switch in the balance of power between TT specialists and climbers

"The reason is simple, although we should put things into perspective, given we're in a world where people don't put things into perspective anymore," Prudhomme told reporters at the presentation, which revealed there'll be a 38-kilometre time trial on stage 7 and a 33-kilometre TT on stage 11.

"It's been 15 years since we've had so much time trialling, during the Tour won by Bradley Wiggins, and this is done with that in mind.

"Since then the riders who won in the time trials have also won in the mountains so it made no sense to extend the TT distances because the same people won, anyway.

"But now that's not the case, we've got different kinds of riders. It's just like back in the very distant era when Federico Bahamontes took time [in the mountains] on Jacques Anquetil," a renowned time trialling specialist.

"Now it's Remco Evenepoel who gains time against the clock, which he may lose in the mountains."

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar"

Prudhomme's comments about Bahamontes and Anquetil regarding balance could also have referred to the 1959 Tour, won by the Eagle of Toledo in part thanks to his crushing domination in a mountain time trial on the Puy de Dôme, where riders like Anquetil were pushed to nearly four minutes back. That said, Anquetil then regained more than five on Bahamontes in the race's final TT to Dijon, a massive 69 kilometres long. But there was some kind of balance, even if Bahamontes had done more than enough to win the Tour outright by that point.

In either case, Prudhomme argued, if Evenepoel was an example for now, it wasn't simply designed to favour one rider in particular. Rather, the question of having a much higher number of time trialling kilometres in 2027 was mainly to ensure that rather than any rider gaining too much of an advantage early on, the suspense could be maintained as long as possible.

"It's a question of resetting the balance, not for the organisers but all the fans who want there to be a fight right the way to the end," Prudhomme explained.

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar, you put pavé or time trials or climbs in front of him, he can take time and then he gains even more time on his rivals on the descents," he added, in reference to what Pogačar did on the descent of the Tourmalet on stage 6 last July, doubling his advantage over Jonas Vingegaard after dropping him close to the summit and all but winning the Tour in the process.

"If he [Pogačar] is stronger, he's stronger," Prudhomme added. "But there is a will to rebalance things, not for a single rider in particular, just like a few years ago we tried to make the route have a more punchy kind of course to try to boost the chances of a spectacular race.

"But in any case," Prudhomme concluded, making a wordplay on an old proverb, "the organisers propose and the riders dispose. That's always true."

"There are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour"

While the increase in time trialling kilometres represented one big change in route trends, Prudhomme argued that the fans should not take it for granted that the mountains in the 2027 race would be a straightforward re-run of other years.

"I hope that people will be surprised, first on paper, then after being surprised on paper, in reality. Because there are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour, and others which have been around but which don't have as fearsome a reputation as they deserve," he told reporters.

"So it's true we've got some classic climbs like the Tourmalet. But I'm thinking especially of the return of the Col de Burdincurutcheta, which is one of the hardest in the French Basque Country," he said of the early climb on stage 19, 8.7km long with average gradients of 9.3%.

"Then the Col du Pré, which is really daunting, too," he added of the Alpine climb, measuring 12.6km at 7.8%, which appears before the final ascent of Saisies on stage 11.

"Then there is the stage across the Massif Central with more than 3,800 metres of vertical climbing through beautiful but tough landscapes.

"Don't forget, too, that in the first week we're in Wales, there are climbs that are really hard, right from the gun on stage 3. I know the local people there are very proud of what will be on show in their part of the world that day."

One unusual feature of the Tour de France is its mini-homage to the 2027 UCI Cycling World Championships, the so-called 'Super Worlds', which will take place on the road in the northern Alps in late August and on the track in the Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines velodrome near Paris.

Stage 10 will feature the circuit of the Côte de Domancy and finishes in Sallanches, where the road World Championships also took place in 1980 and will do again in 2027, whilst stage 21 starts in Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines and will go past the velodrome en route to the Champs-Élysées.

"We weren't going ever to do the World Championships before the World Championships actually took place, which is why there will only be two ascents of the Domancy and not 20," Prudhomme explained, "but that's where Bernard Hinault, a legend of the Tour, won the Worlds in 1980, so it's also to honour him."

"The climbs there aren't very high up, but the slopes are something special: short but really, really tough. So there will be lots to see that day, too."

And perhaps, too, in the time trials as well.

items.title: Anti-Pogačar? Not quite, but this radical Tour de France route does highlight ASO's love-hate relationship with the world's best rider
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
You might have seen the 2027 Tour de France route described as an 'anti-Pogačar' exercise, and, with a return to time trialling doses of old and a relatively meagre helping of high mountains, you can certainly see why.

In truth, there is no such thing as an 'anti-Pogačar' route. It simply does not exist within the realms of plausible conception. It would have to be 21 flat stages, half of them against the clock, and even then he’d still probably find a way to win.

And yet, the route that was unveiled in Paris on Thursday did signal a growing discomfort, on the part of the Tour de France organisers, with Tadej Pogačar’s dominance. Jonas Vingegaard’s epic takedowns of the Slovenian are three years in the past now, and Pogačar has since rattled off a trio of yellow jerseys, each more convincing than the last, to take his tally to a record-equalling five.

He has done so with the sort of panache the race directors can only dream of, but he has also done it with a level of ease that is becoming a bit of a nightmare. So utterly superior, Pogačar spent the second half of this year’s Tour essentially riding as a domestique for his third-placed teammate, Isaac del Toro. In some ways, the yellow jersey selflessly repaying favours is a nice image for the race. In others ways, it’s really not such a great look – not one you’d want to make a habit of, anyway.

The irony was that the 2026 Tour de France had been billed as a 'Tour of Suspense'. The route had been constructed in such a way, we were told, that the battle for yellow would only be decided in the final days on Alpe d’Huez. As it turned out, Pogačar had the jersey all but sewn up by stage 6.

I wrote a piece on this at the time – about how the attempt to tone down the early Col du Tourmalet only toned it up – so I won’t rehash it all here, but it was a bit of an own goal, I felt. Granted, Pogačar’s dominance would have told anyway, but in any case, it was revealing in the broader context of ASO’s intentions.

Put simply, they badly want a yellow jersey contest that remains open until the last few days, and it didn’t work last time.

Not a good year to be a polka-dot fan

And so here we are, not going above 1,750 metres of altitude until stage 18 of 21 next July.

The route for that stage is a Pyrenean beast – going over the Soulor, Tourmlaet, and Hourquette d’Ancizan before the final climb to the Col du Portet – but it makes everything else look pretty tame in comparison. In fact, it’s only the second of two true mountain-top finishes in the entire race.

The Alps have had it pretty good in recent years but what did they do to deserve this? Even if the World Champs-inspired stage 10 looks like a thriller and the stage 11 combo of the Col du Pré and Montée de Bisanne looks tough enough, the lack of big-name high-altitude Alpine passes is really quite shocking.

And the Pyrenees may have the upper hand this time but they too only have two stages. Elsewhere, it’s over to the Jura to provide the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier on stage 9, and the Massif Central on a stage 14 that is harder than it looks but still very much sloggy medium mountain stuff. All in all, then, not a good year to be a die-hard polka-dot fan.

And then there’s the time trialling, with 71km against the clock constituting the most ITT-heavy Tour de France since the former world TT champion Bradley Wiggins won the race in 2012. This itself is remarkable, a complete laying down of arms in the battle ASO has waged on time trialling over the past decade. This was, of course, inspired by the dominance of Team Sky – first through Wiggins and then through Chris Froome and Geraint Thomas – but the trend has remained even in the Pogačar and Vingegaard era.

Until now. It’s no coincidence that the runner-up this year is also the best time triallist in the world, by a country mile. Remco Evenepoel may well wear the yellow jersey in next year’s Tour, and he may well take a minute or two on Pogačar, though it’s worth remembering he was beaten by more than six this summer (with Pogačar taking his foot off the gas at times).

So you can’t Pogačar-proof a Tour de France route, but in completely upending the balance between mountains and time trials, the organisers have certainly taken a new, much bolder, step in attempting to prevent him completely running away with it.

Pro-Pogačar, anti-Vingegaard?

At this point, it’s worth circling back to ASO’s relationship with Pogačar, which we might describe as 'love-hate'. They hate the suspense he takes away from the race as a whole, but they absolutely love just about everything else about him.

Race director Christian Prudhomme and co barely made any attempt to hide their distaste of the so-called Skybots, and what an antidote they’ve since struck upon with Pogačar, an all-action figure who will light up the race given even the slightest invitation, or even the slightest hint of boredom. For two years in a row now he has been in the thick of the action on the remodelled final stage over the Montmartre climb in Paris, carrying the Classics torch that has seen him win Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, and twice podium Paris-Roubaix.

In that respect, this is actually quite a pro-Pogačar route. The entire first week is peppered with punchy climbs and Classics-flavoured stages that aren’t critical GC flashpoints but may well tempt Pogačar out to play. The first of the two Alpine stages, based on the route for World Championships past and future, looks like the sort of circuit-based, short-but-hard-climb affair Pogačar would draw up in his dreams.

The marquee high-mountain stages have been toned down only because the terrain dictates that this is where his superiority stretches into big time differences. But for all Pogačar is the best climber in the world, he’s not a pure climber, and he has famously come unstuck on some of the Tour’s most brutal mountain stages. Vingegaard was the man to crack him in both 2022 and 2023, and while the Dane hasn’t come close in recent years, he has mitigating circumstances, not least the fact that he didn’t get to finish this year’s race.

For many years now, Vingegaard has banged out the same old refrain – that he can only try and live with Pogačar on the punchier climbing days, and that he needs the bigger, heavier, multi-col mountain days to truly take the fight to him.

In that light, the 2027 Tour de France route only reduces the room for manouevre for the greatest rival of Pogačar’s career. Of course, with Paul Seixas coming through, that title could change hands at some point, and it’s worth noting that the French prodigy – already a winner at Il Lombardia and runner-up at Liège and Strade Bianche – is cut from very much the same cloth as Pogačar.

But no, if this route is anti-anyone, it’s anti-Vingegaard. And if you were the Dane, seeing your favored terrain neglected as Evenepoel’s is pandered to – by people who want a closer challenge to Pogačar – you might just take that personally.

As for main man himself, we return to the point we made at the start of this piece; you could devise 100 different Tour de France routes, and the Tadej Pogačar of the past three years would win every single time, provided he stays upright.

And here again Prudhomme made a revealing comment. "There are certainly questions lingering after his crash," the race director said of Pogačar’s season-ending Vuelta fall, even going as far as to reference Eddy Merckx’s famous (and much more severe) 1969 crash, after which he was supposedly never the same rider (but still won four more Tours). Prudhomme seems excited by that prospect of a slightly-less-than-perfect Pogačar, or at least relishing the doubt, the intrigue, the… suspense.

Whether we actually get any of the stuff next July remains to be seen. The Tour de France organisers love Tadej Pogačar, but they hate him too, and it seems even clearer now that they want the best of best worlds – to encourage his firework-lighting instincts while at the same time trying to rein him in to some degree.

In that respect, the 2027 Tour de France route is one of the most radical we’ve seen in years – it simply might not make a blind bit of difference.

items.title: 'I'm certainly not opposed to it' – Tim Merlier gives cautious thumbs up to teammate Paul Magnier joining him at 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Triple 2026 Tour de France stage winner Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) has given a cautious welcome to the idea that up-and-coming French sprinter and teammate Paul Magnier might join him in the 2027 race.

Next July, it might be that the two race together in a Grand Tour for the first time.

At the Tour presentation this Thursday, Merlier himself played down the number of sprint stages on offer in the 2027 route but he did not roundly reject the idea of sharing those opportunities with Merlier.

"I have already discussed that with the team," Merlier said in comments reported by . "I am certainly not opposed to it. I think it would be possible.

"He is still young and I have the feeling that he still looks up to me; he sometimes still asks for tips. He could learn a lot from it."

Although the Belgian star argued that it was not necessarily a given that it would happen, concluding on that subject – and without explaining why – that “the chance that it actually happens seems quite small to me".

The other big subject on the virtual table for Merlier in Paris was whether he could take the yellow jersey in Carlisle at the end of day 1 of the 2027 Tour. Opportunities for sprinters to take the opening stage's yellow jersey are never high in the Tour and the sprint finish in Carlisle is a gradual uphill, exactly the kind that Merlier likes.

Furthermore, after missing out in Lille in 2025, the previous chance the fast men had to go for yellow in the Tour, Merlier recognised that he was looking forward to a fresh chance coming his way.

“It would be wonderful. I let it slip in Lille in 2025, so I’m happy to get a second chance already. Normally, that doesn’t happen very often," he said.

"It's a nice challenge for the sprinters, and it's not impossible it could happen."

It might sound surprising that Merlier was pleased that there were two time trials in the 2027 route, but that was more for practical reasons because he was suddenly going to switch specialities at 33. At the same time, he agreed with Mark Cavendish that if the sprinters' teams worked well enough, the last day over the Butte Montmartre in Paris could still end up being decided by a mass dash to the line on the Champs Élysées.

"Two time trials are two rest days for me," he reasoned, "and though I'd like to see a 'real' sprint without the Montmartre on the last day, if the sprinters' teams all work well together, it might still be possible that it happens."

It is true, too, that stage 21 breakaway winner Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech) only took the last dash for the line in Paris by the bare minimum ahead of teammate Jasper Philipsen last July. But in any case, rather than the seven sprints predicted by the Tour de France organisation on Thursday for 2027, Merlier says that he thinks a much smaller number is likely.

"If we can sprint four times, that would already be great. It all looks very tough. When you see the elevation gain [53,450 metres - Ed.] across the race, you don't get very excited as a sprinter," he said with a laugh.
