items.title: Tour de France 2027 route - The complete stage-by-stage guide
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
The 2027 Tour de France ventures into the United Kingdom for the Grand Départ in Scotland on July 2, and two long stages - to Liverpool and through Wales - before the race lands on home soil.

There are two individual time trials, two major summit finishes, six stages for the sprinters and a load of opportunities for attacks through the Alps, Massif Central and Pyrenees before the race concludes in Paris on July 25 after almost 3,500 kilometres of racing.

Tadej Pogačar will be vying for a record sixth Tour title, but will be challenged by Remco Evenepoel over the 71 kilometres of time trials and by Jonas Vingegaard in the high mountains.

A relatively flat start to the Tour de France could see the first sprinter in the maillot jaune in years, but it's a long and complicated road that's not entirely flat, with some punchy climbs and wind that could foil the sprinters.

  • Côte de Melrose (2.2km at 6.7%), km. 65

This stage is quite long at 223 kilometres and riddled with small climbs that will hamper the sprinters' ability to enjoy the relatively flat finish in Liverpool.

  • Côte de Jubilee Tower (3.8km at 6.1%), km. 88
  • Côte de Trough of Bowland (1.9km at 5.2%), km. 98.5
  • Côte de Waddington Fell (3.4km at 6.4%), km. 112
  • Côte de Belmont (2km at 4%), km. 152.5
  • Côte de Parbold (1.8km at 5.6%), km. 183

Someone should make a one-day Classic out of this 223-kilometre stage from Welshpool to Cardiff. With seven named climbs and a couple of real stingers like the 11% Hengoed climb in the late stages, this one could get very interesting for the GC contenders if they haven't studied up on the style of racing.

  • Côte d'Epynt (3.7km at 7.9%), km. 85.5
  • Côte de Bannau Brycheiniog (6.6km at 3.5%), km. 121.5
  • Côte de Rhigos (4.6km at 5.8%), km. 145.5
  • Côte de Penrhys (1.3km at 10.1%), km. 160.5
  • Côte de Maerdy (1.5km at 8.7%), km. 169
  • Côte de Hengoed (700 m at 11%), km. 197.5
  • Côte de Caerphilly (2km at 8.1%), km. 210.5

A punchy stage to Plumelec is one for the powerful sprinters like Mads Pedersen or Matthew Brennan. The Côte de Cadoudal (1.7km at 6.2%) is climbed twice at the end.

  • Côte de la Croix de la Libération (4.6km at 5.3%), km. 189
  • Signal d'Uchon (5.7km at 5.7%), km. 206.5

One of just two high-altitude summit finishes, the stage to Grand Colombier on stage 9 will be one of the key moments of the 2027 Tour de France.

  • Col du Berthiand (6.3km at 7.5%), km. 57.5
  • Côte des Neyrolles (3.6km at 7.7%), km. 77
  • Col de Richemond (7.7km at 6%), km. 115
  • Grand Colombier (17.4km at 7.1%), km. 162

A preview of the combined 2027 UCI World Championships, stage 10 features the Côte de Domancy twice out of six climbs, making for a tough stage that could well bring some surprises.

  • Col du Plan du Salève (9.6km at 5.4%), km. 26
  • Montée de Brison (5km at 10.2%), km. 74
  • Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%), km. 111.5
  • Montée du Bettex (5.5km at 8%), km. 126.5
  • Côte du Plateau d'Assy (5.1km at 7.5%), km. 147.5
  • Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%), km. 162

The third of a difficult string of stages, the finish at le Saisies is just past the summit of the Montée de Bisanne - a fairly steep 12.5km ascent averaging 8.3%. This one has Pogačar written all over it.

  • Col de la Colombière (15.9 km at 7%), km. 16
  • Col de la Croix Fry (7.2 km at 5.5%), km. 40
  • Col de la Forclaz de Queige (5.1 km at 8.2%), km. 85
  • Col du Pré (12.6 km at 7.8%), km. 113
  • Montée de Bisanne (12.4 km at 8.3%), km. 146

The finish in Mende on the Côte de la Croix Neuve a.k.a. Montée Jalabert has produced memorable finishes, starting with Laurent's victory in 1995. It was the place where Joaquim Rodriguez managed to get the better of Alberto Contador in 2010, and where Steve Cummings gave the African team MTN-Qhubeka their first Tour stage win in 2015. Michael Matthews was the last winner here in 2022, but the approach is far more difficult in 2027.

  • Col du Vent (8.4 km at 5.8%), km. 40.5
  • Col de la Lusette (11.6 km at 7.3%), km. 108.5
  • Côte de l'Estrade (5.7 km at 8.3%), km. 175
  • Côte de la Croix Neuve (3 km at 10.1%), km. 197.5

The second individual time trial of the Tour on stage 16 is 33km long and mostly flat, except for a single categorised climb, the Côte de Pech David - a short but steep ascent - in the second half of the race. It only climbs 100m but it does so over just 800m of tarmac.

  • Côte de Pech David (800 m at 12.4%), km. 24

The queen stage of the 2027 Tour de France, stage 18 from Pau to the Col du Portet takes riders over 2000 metres in altitude twice - the first time over the Col du Tourmalet midway through the 174km stage, and then at the finish, with two other medium mountains for good measure.

  • Col du Soulor (11.8 km at 7.3%), km. 50
  • Col du Tourmalet (19 km at 7.4%), km. 106.5
  • Hourquette d'Ancizan (8.2 km at 5.1%), km. 140.5
  • Saint-lary-soulan Col du Portet (16 km at 8.7%), km. 174

The climbing continues on stage 19 with four major ascents including the last chance for glory on the Col de Marie Blanque with 18.5km to go. It's the last major mountain of the Tour since the penultimate stage has been given to the sprinters.

  • Col de Burdincurutcheta (8.7 km at 9.3%), km. 44.5
  • Col de Bagargui (4.8 km at 6.4%), km. 52.5
  • Col de Soudet (15.1 km at 7.2%), km. 95.5
  • Col de Marie Blanque (7.7 km at 8.6%), km. 141.5

After much debate, the Montmartre climb ended up in the final stage of the Tour de France in Paris, with riders tackling the hill, that made its debut in pro cycling during the Olympic Games in 2024, three times. In 2026, the sprinters very nearly caught Mathieu van der Poel, but he held on just long enough to win the stage over teammate Jasper Philipsen.

  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 74
  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 90
  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 106

items.title: Jonas Rutsch and Patrick Eddy add experience for Classics charge for Modern Adventure Factor Racing in 2027
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Australian road race national champion Patrick Eddy and German WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch were confirmed as new additions to Modern Adventure Factor Racing in 2027, each signing a one-year contract.

They will join former USPro under-23 road race national champion Owen Cole, who moves from Team Winston Salem-Flow for the next two seasons.

The team debuted at the ProTour level this past season with 20 of the 21 riders signed to two-year deals. Leo Hayter, who was the only team member confirmed for 2026, recently renewed to continue in the burgundy and gold colours through 2027.

Eddy competed as a U23 rider at the Picnic-PostNL programme, earning a promotion from the development squad to the WorldTour team from 2024 to 2025. He competed at the Continental level in 2026 for a breakout year, starting with the Australian title, and then, with Team Brennan, won the overall at Ronde de l'Oise and the Dutch one-day races Midden-Brabant Poort Omloop and Ronde van Overijssel.

"We're thrilled to welcome Jonas to Modern Adventure. He's built for races like Paris-Roubaix and the classics and he brings a whole new level of experience to our team," team Co-founder George Hincapie said in a team press release.

"Pat had a brilliant season, and winning the Australian national title says a lot about the level he’s capable of. He’s also shown he can deliver results in Europe, which is an important quality for our program."

Both Rutsch and Eddy have extensive experience with European racing, that depth important for the team to bolster their Classics campaign.

The US-based squad remains focused on developing North American talent as well and the addition of Cole brings the number of US and Canadian riders to 14.

The 22-year-old from Chapel Hill, North Carolina, joins the team after continuing to establish himself as a versatile young talent. After winning the U23 road national title in 2023, he moved to UAE Team Emirates Gen Z for European racing, earning a podium on the time trial stage at Tour of Sharjah. He returned to a US-based squad for the last two seasons, winning three silver medals at US nationals, as well as a second place on the Mont Mégantic queen stage at Tour de Beauce and GC title at Tour de la Guadeloupe.

“Joining this team as an American feels extra special. Not only is it an organization I think can take me to the next level, it is a project I look forward to being able to say I was a part of,” Owen said in a team statement.

This brings the Modern Adventure Factor roster to 24 riders for 2027, with a final announcement expected next week.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar tops all UCI rankings but one, while Demi Vollering equally dominant in 2026
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
For the sixth year in a row, Tadej Pogačar has ended the season as the number one rider in the UCI World Rankings, and his UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad were at the top of the Team Rankings for the fourth straight year.

On the women's side, FDJ United-SUEZ topped the UCI Team Rankings for women for the second year in a row, with World Champion and Tour de France winner Demi Vollering crushing the competition in the individual rankings.

Pogačar and Vollering were nearly tied on points accumulated through the season, with 9,331.75 and 9,330 points, respectively, after both had equally dominant seasons with victories in the Tour de France, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Tour of Flanders.

While Vollering had a nearly flawless season, with wins in the Giro d'Italia, Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, La Flèche Wallonne and the World and European Championships road races, Pogačar's season was cut short due to a crash in the Vuelta a España, which meant he gained no points in the World and European Championships.

Still, Pogačar amassed far more points than second-placed Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who ended the year with the World and European time trial titles, second place in the Tour de France and 7,191.61 points. Next in line were Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates XRG) and Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) with 5,606 and 5,580 points, respectively.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe were the second-best team, but were over 5,000 points shy of Pogačar's squad, with Visma-Lease a Bike, Decathlon CMA CGM and Lidl-Trek rounding out the top five on the men's side.

Behind Vollering in the women's rankings was Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) with 5,660 points, mirroring her results in the Tour de France and World Championships. Paula Blasi and Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team l'IMAD) were third and fourth, and helped their team finish second overall to FDJ by 263 points. SD Worx-Protime, Canyon-SRAM and Visma-Lease a Bike completed the top five. Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) was fifth.

In the minor rankings, Pogačar continued his dominance in the UCI Stage Race Rankings, beating Giro d'Italia winner Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Del Toro, but his three-year winning streak in the UCI One-Day Race Rankings ended because of his crash, and Evenepoel took home that prize for 2026 with Pogačar second and Seixas third.

Pogačar continued to lead the European Tour rankings over Evenepoel and Seixas, but Pinarello-Q36.5 came in as the top team ahead of Tudor and Cofidis. Belgium led the nations rankings.

Biniam Girmay (NSN) led the Africa Tour Rankings ahead of fellow Eritreans Natnael Tesfasion (Movistar) and Henok Mulueberhan (XDS Astana). The Algerian team Madar Pro Cycling led the African team rankings, while Eritrea topped the nations.

In the Americas Tour, Del Toro led the individual rankings ahead of Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost), with World Champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) third and, thanks to his rainbow jersey-winning effort, the USA led the nations rankings. Modern Adventure led the team rankings.

Yevgeniy Fedorov (XDS Astana) finished out the year atop the Asia Tour rankings as did his native Kazakhstan, while the Chinese team Li Ning Star led the teams. In Oceania, it was Laurence Pithe, Jai Hindley and Michael Matthews atop the individual rankings, Australia as top nation and CCache X Bodywrap the number one team.

There are no Continental tours for women.

items.title: 'Some haggis and a deep-fried Mars Bar' - Local star Oscar Onley highlights Scottish specialities ahead of 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Tour de France contender Oscar Onley says he is counting the days to the race's start in Scotland, where the GC specialist will be looking forward to what he calls a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" to race cycling's biggest professional event on home soil.

In the meantime, too, he's got every intention highlighting some specialities in the local diet to Tour de France followers who may be unfamiliar with Scottish culinary traditions.

Asked at the Tour de France presentation in Paris on Thursday what people can expect as a Scottish welcome, Onley said - half-jokingly - "Some haggis and a deep-fried Mars Bar, that'd be the go-to.

"It'll be really special, I think, particularly because of the crowds, they always get behind the big sporting events and I expect the same thing next year as well.

"It's something I couldn't even have dreamed of, normally the Tour de France is in France, so it's a once-in-a lifetime opportunity. I really want to hopefully be there, and that's my first goal."

Fourth in the 2025 Tour de France was a breakthrough result for Onley, but then injuries incurred in a major crash on a descent on stage 7 of the Critérium du Dauphiné put paid to his chances of racing it this summer.

Onley subsequently bounced back to take fourth overall in the Vuelta a España, but he denied that there was any extra pressure on him to perform as Ineos have such a significant series of past success in the Tour de France.

"I don't think so. As riders we all put a lot of pressure on ourselves, it's more the team do a good job in managing that and making sure we do everything we need to. But they don't add pressure to what we do."

That said, the goal of winning a Grand Tour remains the main objective for Netcompany Ineos, he argued and "the Tour de France is the biggest one, every team has these big ambitions and we're no different.

"I think from what I've seen in the team this year, we're definitely going in the right direction, we have all the resources to make something like this happen."

Nor are the past Grand Tour victories a distant memory of glories past, he argues, for Netcompany Ineos, with riders who remain in the current lineup also part of the former success in those races.

"Kwiato [Michal Kwiatkowski] is still in the team, he's also been part of a lot of these Tour-winning teams. He's always got lots of stories of training camps and races as well, and it's quite inspiring when he says these things over dinner to us."

The route for 2027 is now out, in any case, and Onley is convinced that having that knowledge so soon, nearly seven months before the event actually starts in Edinburgh next July 2, can only be a good thing. He hasn't yet pinpointed one stage as one that suits him particularly well - although he's certain that'll happen. Rather the idea is to stay in the action in the race from start to finish.

"There are opportunities everywhere, everyone's got weaknesses and strengths and it's better to know the course now, you can really prepare for what's ahead," he reasoned.

"It's not like no-one knows the parcours. There are no excuses for July."

items.title: 'Where is the Tour de France Hommes?' - Marlen Reusser calls for greater equality between men’s and women’s Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
2026 Tour de France Femmes leader and stage winner Marlen Reusser has made a call to step up the fight for parity between men's and women's cycling, arguing that a great deal has been done but that there are still steps to be taken.

The Movistar leader said she had enjoyed the race presentation in Paris, but argued that there was a greater level of protagonism for the men's event during it than the women's. She also asked why the men's event was not called the Tour de France Hommes to balance it out with the Tour de France Femmes.

ASO organiser Marion Rousse responded to her comments by saying that the race had taken major steps towards a much greater level of equality - something which Reusser had already underlined - but that both the races had to evolve at the same rate as the sport in general. She also pointed out that the Tour de France Femmes presentation was shorter, that was connected to the different length of the events.

Reusser said that she had felt inspired by the route presentation, recalling the time when she had been to a similar kind of event for the Olympics and it had considerably boosted her interest in the event.

"The presentation was really cool, I remember doing after only I was a very short time in cycling, doing the Olympic Games and it was never something I was dreaming about or something, but then I had to go to the kick-off, it was kind of this event in Switzerland for the Olympic Games and I was so infected by the Olympic spirit," she explained.

"So I wanted to come here to see if I get infected and I think that they managed well. It's a nice event."

At the same time, she said, it would be good if things continued to develop in term of the fight for equality between the two events, starting off with their name.

"But I'm a bit disappointed still that it's Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes, where is the Tour de France Hommes? This is weird to me, this I don't understand. Also like we have two nice directors, but I don't feel like it's them on the same level, it's more the men's director that is [on stage] then also having next to him the women's, " she said.

"So I think the Tour is doing so great showing that there is not only men's sport, but then we speak a lot about it but we just should do it more. I wish these little steps to come when we speak about the presentation and the whole thing."

Asked about Reusser's comments, Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse argued categorically that there had been a great deal of progress, but warned against taking decisions too fast that could potentially do more harm than good in the long run. She also pointed to the Tour de France Grand Départ in the UK as being a key balancing act between the two races.

"It's already a big first to start in the same country outside the Tour de France, and the United Kingdom is a natural step, because they have already done a lot of work developing with women's sport, with things like the Rugby World Cup in 2025 or the Women's Tour of Britain," Rousse argued. "We're doing exactly the same thing in the UK, three days for the men, three days for the women - it's magnificent.

"We also will continue the work, but there's also the question of continuing to develop the race at the same pace as women's sport. If we suddenly do 15 days of racing tomorrow" - as opposed to the nine in the race as is the case for 2027 - "of course the women are able to do that, but certain teams would find that hard.

"We want to show what women's cycling is capable of doing and that's done, the sponsors are investing and the tv exposure is happening, that's all done. We are going to go on evolving, but we have to be careful, because once a step is taken you can't go back. Each decision is important."

Regarding any perceived imbalance between the men's and the women's presentation, she argued that that was "not really the case, because obviously the men's presentation is going to be longer because there are 21 stages against nine.

"But if not the work is exactly the same and besides we are doing the same thing, it's just there are fewer stages."

items.title: No time trial, Alps, or Pyrenees and a finale that might be without fans – I was left wanting more from the Tour de France Femmes route reveal
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
In 2026, the Tour de France Femmes seemed to get everything right. After four years of experimentation, the route felt like ASO had pulled together everything they'd learnt into a beautifully balanced course, featuring a bit of everything: a foreign Grand Départ, an iconic mountain stage, a time trial, and a big-city finale.

The result was a truly thrilling race, delivering six different stage winners, five different riders in the yellow jersey, and a GC battle that went down to the wire on the very last day.

There were limitations, of course, for example the geographical footprint of the race was small, with much of France not getting a chance to by the roadside. But with what ASO and race director Marion Rousse can do with nine days of racing, they seemed to get it pretty spot on.

Fast forward to this year, then, and the expectation around the route reveal was high. How could they build upon perhaps the best edition of the Tour de France Femmes yet? How would they raise the bar again this time, as they have in every other edition? We were surely in for another cracking route.

But when Marion Rousse was done presenting the nine stages that will make up next year's Tour to the Palais de Congrès audience and fans around the world, I was left feeling a bit flat.

My initial reaction to the stage featuring the iconic Puy de Dôme climb was excitement – 'Wow, they're really doing it' – but as the screen faded to black to confirm that was the final stage, my feeling shifted more to 'Oh, is that it?'.

Though not an icon of the 21st century – it was only reintroduced in full to the Tour in 2023 after a 35-year absence – the Puy de Dôme occupies an important place in Tour history, the site of some truly memorable battles, not least when Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor went literally shoulder to shoulder on the ascent in 1964. Its iconic shape, rising up above Clermont-Ferrand, and the railway following the riders up its slopes gives it a clear and looming identity.

But it's also only 11.3km, only climbs up to 1,415m, and isn't on the level of fame nor difficulty of some of the iconic Pyrenean or Alpine passes. In fact, no climb on the whole 2027 Tour de France Femmes route surpasses 1,500m elevation, let alone the benchmark 2,000m, something you can only get in the Alps and Pyrenees.

It's not that the final three stages aren't packed full of climbing – they are – but there's only so much you can do in France's third biggest mountain range.

Of course, there is a reason to skip the Pyrenees and Alps: the organisers like to change things up each year, and they are also slightly hamstrung by the UK Grand Départ, making the Massif Central much more reasonable to journey to in only a week, compared to going all the way south to either bigger mountain range.

But having seen the true mountain battles we've been treated to for the last few years, the Massif Central – literally and figuratively – just doesn't reach those heights.

In this day and age, 1,400m cannot be the ceiling of how high the Tour de France Femmes can climb. We've known since this race was launched that big, iconic mountains are what make it special, and what deliver the truly showpiece days, like Mont Ventoux earlier this summer.

I have no doubt that this Massif Central-focused course will be challenging, engaging and thrilling, and we'll see another brilliant battle for the yellow jersey – I just wish we were doing it on some bigger, better climbs, more akin to what we've seen before.

It's also an undeniable shame that this race is missing an individual time trial, opting for a team time trial in London as part of the Grand Départ instead. As I wrote in my route explainer, the Tour is limited in time and they can't do everything – at least not in the sense that the men's race can, with a whole 21 stages to play with – so something always has to be dropped.

But is a team time trial really preferable to an individual time trial? It's novel, sure, having never been done in the Tour de France Femmes before, and it's perhaps slightly more fun for casual fans for watch. It also shortens the amount of time that the race will have to close roads in central London for. But is it good for the race?

The results of a TTT will naturally be very different from an ITT, arguably levelling out the playing field between the top riders – they are all both supported and limited by their teammates, so we're unlikely to see a Reusser for example take a bit chunk of time here – but at the same time disproportionately disadvantaging those on smaller teams.

We haven't often seen underdogs come to the fore in the Tour, and including a TTT – which the better-resourced teams always do better in – basically ensures we definitely won't in 2027.

But really, the main issue is that I just think the Tour should have a TT, always. The concept of a men's Tour de France without a time trial is basically unconscionable, and whilst the women's race in only nine stages, it purports to be a Grand Tour, and that should mean the winner has to face a bit of everything: time trialing, sprints, hills and mountains – that's what makes a Grand Tour and a Grand Tour winner.

Riders and teams have long been in agreement on that fact, and have complained when other women's Grand Tours have missed a TT, so for the Tour to go back to a TT-less form feels like a downgrade on last year. A team time trial just isn't the same.

The other really concerning element of the Femmes route reveal is the question over whether fans will be allowed on the Puy de Dôme summit finish.

When the men's race last visited, in 2023, fans were not allowed on the final 4km due to ecological protections, and also the difficulty in getting up the climb that only has one road up, which is flanked on one side by an in-use railway line. That meant the finale of the climb was raced in an eerie absence of spectators, with even very few media at the top to capture the moment, something that perhaps doesn't feel befitting of the biggest race on earth.

But even the risk of having no fans on the final, decisive climb of the race feels fundamentally antithetical to everything the Tour de France Femmes has been building for the last five years. The whole project has been based around , bringing fans out, making the event as big and as accessible as possible to show just how much appetite there is for women's racing.

Mont Ventoux this year was a spectacular example of that, with fans lining every kilometre of the Bald Mountain, making the long journey up to its moon-like peak. The fans are what have made this race so special and successful, and has always been at the heart of the event.

So to not have fans present to cheer on the sport's best athletes on the decisive, climactic climb of next year's race would not just be disappointing, it would be a failure in organisation. We'll all be keeping our fingers crossed that ASO and the local authorities find a solution, but if they don't, and we have a fan-free finale to the biggest race on earth next summer, serious questions will have to be asked over the decisionmaking around going to this particular climb.

I thought that ASO finally cracked the formula on how to do it all within nine days in 2026, but 2027's route has shown us that truly doing a little bit of everything, including a TT, and going to one of the big two mountain ranges, is still a stretch for this race. Which is understandable, but when we've seen how good it can be, it's hard to not feel a little shortchanged.

I know the race will deliver, it always does, but on paper, it's left a lot to be desired.

items.title: 'I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider’ - Mountain bike star Jolanda Neff makes surprise move to Fenix-Premier Tech
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Former mountain bike world and Olympic champion Jolanda Neff will ride on the Fenix-Premier Tech squad for two years from 2027, the Belgian team have announced.

At 33-years-old, the Swiss rider is experienced across road and cyclo-cross, but she is best known for her exploits on the mountain bike, a discipline where she has gained a wealth of success.

Not only did she win Olympic gold in Tokyo, she was cross-country World Champion in 2017 and the cross-country MTB Marathon rainbow jersey winner the year before that. She also boasts 16 elite World Cup race victories in her career.

While Neff might not have been quite as successful on the cyclo-cross field, she has a total of 11 wins, with two last season when she was competitive in every race she rode.

On the road, Neff has never won above .2 level, but as long ago as 2014 she bagged third place at Trofeo Alfredo Binda, then a top-level World Cup race, and was fourth and fifth on general classification at the UCI Women’s WorldTour stage race, Tour de Suisse, in 2021 and 2022, respectively.

Neff has raced the last two mountain bike campaigns for the Cannondale Factory Racing outfit, but that team’s demise, which coincides with the company’s move to the Netherlands, has forced her to seek a team elsewhere, and Fenix-Premier Tech seems a good fit.

"I’m really excited to join Fenix-Premier Tech, a team that unites mountain biking, cyclocross and road racing at a world-class level," Neff said in a team statement.

"I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider in every aspect, as well as sharing all my experience with other riders. I have always admired how this team puts a strong focus on women and on creating professional structures for them, as well as developing young riders with a long-term vision. I hope to make a great contribution to Fenix-Premier Tech and can’t wait to get racing!"

Fenix-Premier Tech and their brother team Alpecin-Premier Tech, are a true multi-discipline outfit with a number of riders throughout the roster riding both on and off-road. On the women’s side alone, the team boasts cyclo-cross World Cup race winners Aniek van Alphen and Puck Pieterse, as well as former World Champion Ceylin de Carmen Alvarado. Pieterse is also a past mountain bike World Champion, and has won the best young rider and mountains classifications at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, along with a handful of top Classics.

items.title: Visma say 'there could have been more' summit finishes on 2027 Tour de France route, but remain certain of opportunities for two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike see plenty of opportunities for their leaders at the 2027 Tour de France, where they will likely be led by two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard, who crashed out of this year's edition, Wout van Aert, and potentially sprinter Matthew Brennan.

After the route was revealed on Thursday in Paris, Head of Racing Marc Reef commented on the 21 stages, where two time trials, six mountain stages, and a brutal queen stage in the Pyrenees are set to decide the next yellow jersey.

“At first glance, it looks like a fairly balanced route, with several flat sprint stages, explosive finales and tough mountain stages," said Reef.

"The two long, relatively flat time trials stand out in particular. It’s been a long time since we’ve had that in the Tour. Compared to last year, I count fewer summit finishes, and in my opinion, there could have been more. All in all, it’s an interesting route."

To Reef's point, there are only three summit finishes on the 2027 course: stage 9 to Grand Colombier, stage 11 to Les Saisies, and stage 18 to Saint-Lary-Soulan Col du Portet.

On paper, it's a route more in favour of this year's runner-up Remco Evenepoel than Vingegaard, but it's defending champion Tadej Pogačar that both riders will be looking to knock off top spot in July.

Reef noted how important the two time trials will be for GC, totalling 71 kilometres, but also how the days to Sallanches and up the Col du Portet will be crucial as Vingegaard looks to defeat Pogačar for the first time since 2023.

"[Stages 9 to 11 are] where the GC contenders will go head-to-head for the first time. These are stages that could suit us well. Racing on the World Championships course also adds an extra dimension to the Tour," he said.

“The last time we had this many [ITT kilometres] was in 2012. On top of that, most of the courses are relatively flat. Time trialling is a discipline we work on extensively and invest a lot in. We’re generally very strong in this area, and we have several specialists on the team. These races against the clock will play a major role in the general classification.

The Pyrenees duo of stages are "where the race will be decided”, according to Reef, on stages 18 and 19. With 5,400m of elevation gain on the former, it's not only the hardest stage of the 114th edition, but one of the most difficult in recent memory, and would be somewhere where a top-form Vingegaard should thrive.

"Some television viewers may find it harder to relate to the climbs on this year’s Tour de France route, but there are still some fantastic stages. The finishes atop the Grand Colombier and Col de Portet are certainly ones to look forward to. The final stage in Paris is another highlight, of course," said Reef.

"It looks like a route that should suit several of our riders very well. Our task now is to analyse the route thoroughly and use that analysis to develop a plan that gives us the best possible chance of success as a team. One thing is certain: this route offers us plenty of opportunities to achieve great things."

The Tour kicks off on July 2 in 2027, with a flat stage from Edinburgh in Scotland to Carlisle in England, where they could bring Brennan as a debutant, alongside his superstar lead-out man from the Vuelta, Van Aert – who will no doubt get his own opportunities on the plethora of punchy stages – and target the first yellow jersey with the Brit on home roads.

items.title: Local authorities to decide if spectators allowed on Puy de Dôme climb in Tour de France Femmes, say organisers
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
In the equivalent 2023 men's event, spectators were prohibited by the authorities on the entirety of the same climb because the site is of special ecological interest.

While the 2023 stage itself saw a thrilling duel unfold on the climb between top favourites Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard, the absence of fans made for a bizarre spectacle, reminiscent of the 2020 Tour de France, where spectators were also banned from many climbs and much of the route because of COVID-19.

The question is arguably even more relevant for the 2027 Tour de France Femmes as the Puy de Dôme is the final climb of the final stage of the race, wheras in 2023, the men's Tour then continued for another 10 days before its final showdown in the Alps and Vosges.

Tour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse told reporters at the race presentation that local authorities would decide on the question of spectators, but insisted, too, that the organisers were merely "tenants of the course" - in other words, they were not permanently attached to it - and as such were very aware of the need to take care of it as well as possible.

"I am sure we're going to take good note of what happened in the Tour finish with [Tadej] Pogačar and [Jonas] Vingegaard; that was very special," Rousse told reporters after the presentation.

In 2023, she recalled, "We went from a race atmosphere at the foot of the col which was full of people, an enormous crowd and suddenly there was absolutely nothing. It was something that both riders and TV commentators really noticed."

Without going into any detail, Rousse promised that "it will be different" this time around.

"An announcement will be made this evening at Puy de Dôme by the regional department because we have done a second race presentation there.

"But we're very conscious about the fact we are simply tenants of the route, and we definitely want this mountain to be preserved as it always has been. So what happens there will be under the direction of the local authorities."

As for the start of the Tour de France Femmes in Scotland and the two stages through England and Wales, Rousse described it as a "historic event".

"It's the first Grand Départ outside France where both the men's and women's Tours start in the same country, and that is already exceptional.

"We really feel that Great Britain wants to develop the women's sport at the same level as men's sport, so there will be equality for men and women in the Grand Départ, three days for both in the same country. That's wonderful."

Rousse said that she had first been inspired by the idea of racing in Great Britain for the Tour De France Femmes by watching the equivalent men's race in 2014 on TV and seeing just how large the crowds were that year. She had, she said, never seen so many people watching the race.

Taking that year's event as inspiration for a Tour de France Femmes Grand Départ in the UK, she said that "I've had this idea in my head for years.

"So when you're telling me that it's time for our race to be there in a few months time, that's marvellous, we're really looking forward to it.

"I truly think the Grand Départ in Great Britain will mark a 'before' and 'after' for the Tour de France Femmes."

items.title: 'There are certainly questions lingering after his crash' – Tour de France director doubts whether Tadej Pogačar can reach his previous level, referencing Eddy Merckx's famous 1969 crash
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme has questioned whether Tadej Pogačar will be the same again after his Vuelta a España crash, saying next year's Tour de France route will put the five-time champion to the test.

The 2027 Tour route was unveiled on Thursday in Paris, with the 21-day race featuring two time trials totalling 71km, seven sprint stages, and just three summit finishes.

Speaking to after the unveiling, Prudhomme said there are "certainly many questions lingering" following Pogačar's Vuelta crash, which left him out of racing for the rest of the year with a concussion, broken collarbone and a fractured vertebra.

"The real question for me – and I obviously wish him all the best – is how well he’ll have recovered from his very, very, very serious crash in the Vuelta a España," Prudhomme said.

"Because his talent lies not only in his physical superiority, but also in his riding skills. His descent of the Tourmalet last summer was mind-blowing and jaw-dropping. As you get older, after such a massive crash, are you still the same person? Do you take as many risks?"

Pogačar remains the overwhelming favourite to win next year's Tour, even if he has fewer chances to gain major time on his opponents. Meanwhile, Remco Evenepoel will eye the two long time trials as personal opportunities.

Prudhomme drew a comparison with another five-time Tour winner, Eddy Merckx, who crashed hard in a derny track race in Blois in 1969, suffering a concussion, displaced pelvis, trapped nerves in his back, among other injuries.

Merckx later said: "Blois was the worst experience of my career. I could have been dead. The accident cost me a few years of my career, because afterwards, with that back, I never had the same feeling uphill as I had in that very first Tour of 1969."

There's no suggestion Pogačar suffered any similar lasting physical damage in his Vuelta crash, though Prudhomme still left it open for debate.

"There are certainly questions lingering after his crash. Whether it has left its mark on him and what the consequences will be," he said.

"Eddy Merckx has always said that he was never the same again after his crash in Blois; he was undoubtedly scarred morally and mentally, but he also says he was never the same in the mountains afterwards.

"But that didn’t stop him from winning four more Tours de France after that," Prudhomme recognised.

items.title: 'An opportunity for the sprinters to pull on a yellow jersey' – Mark Cavendish relishing a sprinter winning stage 1 of the 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Mark Cavendish was one of the many stars of the Tour de France route presentation in Paris on Thursday morning and is looking forward to the opening three stages in Britain next year.

Despite its lumpy start, the 185km first stage between the Scottish capital Edinburgh and the English city of Carlisle may well be one which suits the punchy sprinters, as it flattens out before crossing the border with around 40km to go. And should a sprinter win, they will wear yellow for at least one day.

Cavendish did just that in 2016, winning the opening stage at Utah Beach in Normandy when racing for the Dimension Data squad, and he’s backing another sprinter to repeat that performance at next year’s race.

"I always like when there's an opportunity for the sprinters to pull on a yellow jersey in the first stage of the Tour de France," he said after the presentation.

"I was very fortunate to have that opportunity a couple of times and then pull on the yellow jersey once in my career, and it's really nice to see that on the first stage in the UK.

"Hopefully we can have a winner that'll make a nice story for what will be an incredible weekend."

Cavendish experienced two British Grands Départs during his long career, first in London in 2007 when he raced his maiden Tour, then again in 2014, when he crashed out of contention late in the opening stage in Harrogate. But he believes the British people have a real affinity with the race.

"I think people still talk about it today, 12, 13 years later. Unfortunately, that stage didn't finish as well as I'd hoped, but it was incredible to experience it, and to see the Tour de France go back there," he said.

"I think there's an incredible relationship between France and the UK, and Great Britain really appreciates the Tour de France for being the greatest sporting event on the planet, and you really see that when it goes there.

"To be able to see it in not even just a small portion of the UK, but in Scotland, in England, in Wales, it's very, very spectacular.

"The second stage to Liverpool, actually, if it's a clear day, we'll see my home in the Isle of Man from across the sea, and a lot of the roads I know very well, and I'm really excited to see the excitement for the Tour de France there always is when the Grand Départ is in the UK."

A Pertex 2.5-layer membrane is the highlight, but the two-way zipper and adjustments in fit are also worthy upgrades.

Weather protection is the primary job of any waterproof jacket, and Rapha claims to have elevated the Core III by swapping out the previous model’s proprietary 2.5-layer nylon for a fully seam-taped Pertex 2.5-layer woven fabric. According to Rapha, this textile upgrade delivers a superior balance of waterproof defence, breathability, and long-term durability on the bike.

A two-way zip although a small point is worth is always worth having, making it significantly easier to reach into your jersey pockets or dump heat quickly on climbs without unzipping the top. The Core III now gets a 2-way AquaGuard zipper, and in our opinion, a welcome addition over the single-way zipper on Core II.

Other noteworthy tweaks come in the fit, and Rapha claims to have slightly trimmed around the torso and shoulders to reduce excess flapping fabric while maintaining enough stretch and room for mid-layer insulation (like a jersey or thermal base layer).

Although this Rapha deal is UK-based, Rapha US has all the colours available, and if you're looking for a specific colour out of the seven options available. However, it's full price there at $190.

items.title: Coros launches futuristic Dura 2 Solar computer with monster battery life and built-in voice control
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Coros has launched the new Dura 2 Solar bike computer today, in what is a major update to the brand's original Dura model, which launched in 2024.

The original Dura made waves when it launched thanks to its solar charging technology, which provided at least a 120-hour battery life, making the unit popular with long-distance riders or those who wanted to cut down on regular charging.

The Dura 2 Solar maintains the same claimed 120-hour battery life from a single charge, not including solar power and 2:1 solar regeneration (meaning you gain two hours of battery for every hour of sun exposure) that the original unit had, and there's been a major overhaul everywhere else.

The unit has been redesigned into a slicker, lighter package; the old digital dial is gone, and the hardware has been given a major upgrade.

In short, the Dura 2 Solar seems to be a far more premium overall package that looks more capable of taking the fight to the big hitters when it comes to the best bike computers.

Something else that has changed is the price: the Dura 2 has a retail price of $499 / £429 / €499, a healthy amount more than the previous unit's RRP of $249 and comes without a mount.

The unit uses a horizontal quarter-turn standard (Garmin mount), and the brand argues most riders already have a mount, or need a specific one anyway for their bike's handlebars.

A computer and mount option is available for $549 / £479 / €549, and standard and out-front mounts are available for $79 / £69 / €79.

The unit will be available for purchase from the 27th of October. We understand the original Coros Dura unit will be phased out from this point.

We have everything we know so far here on the computer, as well as our first impressions after logging some rides with the new unit.

Carbon fibre, aluminium and solar power

The Dura 2 Solar looks radically different to the outgoing unit; it's now lighter than before at a claimed 99 grams and uses a T700 carbon fibre backplate and aluminium alloy in its construction.

The front half of the unit is incredibly thin at just 5.7mm, whilst the solar charging panels have been moved to the bottom of the computer. There are two buttons on either side of the computer body, as well as a USB-C charging port on the right-hand side. There are also two new haptic buttons which can be found on the solar panel as well.

The screen is now bigger; the Dura 2 has a 3.5" Sharp MIP (memory-in-pixel) colour touchscreen, an increase over the old unit's 2.7" screen. Coros has provided some details. The screen has a 17:9 aspect ratio and 201 pixels per square inch.

Like the Garmin Edge 1060 computer that launched this week, the Dura 2 also has a voice control feature. Pressing both buttons on the side of the unit activates the voice control feature, which can be toggled on and off.

The unit, as you might expect, is WiFi, ANT+, and Bluetooth-friendly and works with GPS, GLONASS, GALILEO, BDS and QZSS satellite systems. The brand promises improved routing, pinch-to-zoom screen mapping, climb alerts, and offline re-routing.

Routes can be built in the Coros companion app, which also supports a workout planner and training metric analytics features.

There's also a built-in bike bell, media and camera control functionality, and the ability to upload to ChatGPT and Claude for training analysis.

Shimano and SRAM drivetrain support is built in, and Coros says Campagnolo compatibility will come at the end of the year. Third-party app connections can also be made to the likes of Zwift, Wahoo, Strava, Ride with GPS, Komoot, TrainingPeaks and TrainerRoad.

I've been riding with the Dura 2 for a little while and have logged five hours on the unit so far. Aesthetically, it looks pretty cool, sleek and thoroughly modern, the very thin-to-normal body design perhaps looks slightly disjointed, but that's being really picky.

On the lack of a mount coming with the unit, I see no issue. Most riders will have a Garmin-type mount already, and may likely have their own bike specific out-front mounts sorted anyway. It's one less mount in the spares box in my eyes.

After my initial shakedown ride, I fully charged the Dura 2 and, to test the battery, will use it without recharging until I need to.

After five hours of riding and five days of use, I am at 92.9% battery, with a 0.9% solar charge. You can put the unit into sleep mode in about three seconds, or fully turn it off; I've left it asleep for days at a time.

I've been riding with the screen brightness on full, and with PM and HRM sensors paired, for context. It seems safe to say the battery life is considerably bigger than anything else on the market, like the previous unit.

Initially, at unboxing, I was left disappointed by the unit's screen brightness and overall resolution, noting it to be not as vivid or bright as the Karoo or premium Garmin models. In use, this has been less of an issue than I thought it would be, and outdoors on max screen brightness, the screen is perfectly acceptable to me.

The unit is also fast, one of my colleague Josh's key complaints regarding the original Dura was that it was a touch laggy. The touchscreen is very fast and simple to use, as is the overall user interface and processing speed; no issues from me there.

The map layout looks very good, clearer than Garmin units for me, and up there with the best units around. I'm yet to fully test the navigation features, though.

My only other minor issues at this point are that I can't quite figure out how to get my main road activity profile exactly as I want it, and the lap notification screen takes too long to get rid of, but those things will get answered in time.

I'm already grinning at not having to plug the thing in or check the battery, and the unit is proving to be very capable; it also looks darn pretty cool mounted on your bars. Watch this space for a full review.

items.title: Chris Froome predicts a 'closer' Tour de France in 2027
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Four-time Tour de France winner Chris Froome believes we may see a closer contest for the yellow jersey, as he offered his initial take on the 2027 route that was unveiled in Paris on Thursday.

The route features the heaviest dose of time trialling since 2012, when Froome was the runner-up behind his teammate and compatriot Bradley Wiggins, a podium that would preface four Tour titles in the space of five years.

The 71 kilometres of time trialling are not exactly balanced out by a huge dose of mountains, with two stages in the Alps and two in the Pyrenees, and plenty of punchier terrain in between.

For Froome, Tadej Pogačar remains the favourite to win a record sixth title, but might not run away with it in the same way he has in the past three years.

"It is, as usual, a brutal Tour de France. There is really a bit of everything," said Froome, who was in attendance in the Palais des Congrès in Paris and gave his take to the gathered media, including , behind the stage.

"There are more time trial kilometres, that’s also interesting. We have seen the difference Tadej has made in the mountains so maybe with the time trials we’re going to see a bit of a closer race between the favourites. That will change the approach to the race."

Still, it might not change the favourite, with Pogačar already surpassing Froome's four titles with his record-equalling fifth this summer.

"It's just incredible what Tadej has been doing these past few years," Froome said. "I imagine that next year he’ll be lining up as the main favourite for the Tour de France and no doubt going in to challenge for number six."

Froome was also asked about the Grand Départ, which takes place in his home nation of Great Britain, starting in Edinburgh, Scotland and making its way through England and into the Welsh capital of Cardiff before the hop over to France.

"If it’s anything like it was in 2014, the start over in Scotland is going to be amazing," said Froome, who rode as the defending champion the last time the Tour started in Britain, in Yorkshire, 12 years ago.

"The first three stages on UK soil is going to be be something really special. If it’s anything like 2014 it will just be millions and millions of people who come out.

"I never saw a Grand Départ of a Tour de France that was bigger than 2014 so I imagine next year is going to be similar. A lot of colour, a lot of people will really take the opportunity to come out and experience the Tour de France – people who've never been to France to watch the race. I expect millions of people will be on the roads."

items.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 route – The complete stage-by-stage guide
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
The 2027 Tour de France Femmes route takes the peloton from Leeds, England, to the summit of the Puy de Dôme in France's Massif Central, over nine days of racing between July 30 and August 7.

There is no rest day, and the race picks up the following day on French soil with a lightly hilly stage 4 to Calais, followed by a punchy stage 5 to Magnanville, where a series of short climbs in the finale will draw the yellow jersey favourites into battle.

Stage 6 into Bourges is a flat track for the sprinters, but stage 7 is anything but, signalling the first of two mountain summit finishes at La Loge des Gardes, which measures 6.7km at an average gradient of 7.1%.

Stage 8 is net downhill and features a descent to the line, but it's another tough stage through the rugged medium mountains of the Massif Central, where the favourites will be exposed against one another.

Finally, the race will come down to a showdown on the Puy de Dôme, the iconic climb of this volcanic region of central France. Measuring 11.3km on irregular gradients averaging 7.8%, it's a huge test that will decide the yellow jersey at the panoramic summit.

Preview the stage-by-stage details below.

Tour de France Femmes 2025 - Stage by stage guide

  • Côte de Kirkheaton, 1.7km at 7.5%
  • Côte de Meltham, 3.2km at 8.4%
  • Côte de Delph, 2.1km at 6.3%

  • Côte de Calton, 1.6km at 6.3%
  • Winnats Pass, 1.4km at 12.3%
  • Côte de Chunal, 1.4km at 7.1%
  • Snake Pass, 5.4km at 4.6%
  • Côte de Bradfield, 1km at 8.8%
  • Côte d'Oughtibridge, 1.5km at 9.1%
  • Côte de Jenkin Road, 0.8kkm at 10.8%

The Tour de France Femmes will feature a first-ever team time trial on an 18km course in the heart of London on the third day of racing.

  • Palace of Westminster, 0.5km
  • St. Paul's Cathedral, 8km
  • Queen Elizabeth Gate, 13km

  • Côte de Harlettes, 1.1km at 6.9%
  • Côte du Ventus, 1.1km at 6.8%
  • Côte de Bazinghen, 0.9km at 7.5%
  • Côte du Cap Blanc, 0.9km at 7.7%

The fifth day will be a more challenging day featuring eight short, punchy climbs on a 161km race from Neufchâtel-en-Bray to Magnanville. Tour organisers classify the stage as 'flat'.

  • Côte d'Osmoy, 1.6km at 5.2%
  • Côte d'Eawy, 1.8km at 4.5%
  • Côte de Molincourt, 1.6km at 4.4%
  • Côte de Dampsmesnil, 1.5km at 6%
  • Côte de Valcorbon, 1.3km at 5.8%
  • Côte de Baudemont, 1km at 10.2%
  • Côte d'Amenucourt, 1km at 10%
  • Côte de Follainville, 1.1km at 6%

Also classified as a flat stage on the sixth day of racing, the peloton will embark on a 138km from Orléans to Bourges. It is a day for pure sprinters, with no categorised climbs on this stage, but it will also offer some reprieve for the overall contenders before the final three days in the mountains.

The peloton will reach the northern foothills of the Massif Central on the seventh day of racing with a hilly 155km from Nevers to La Loge des Gardes. There are only two categorised ascents on tap, both at the very end, which will surely set the stage for the GC battle on the last two days of racing.

  • Côte du Point du Jour, 2.1km at 8.6%
  • La Loge des Gardes, 6.7km at 7.1%

The Tour de France Femmes will visit Clermont-Ferrand for a third time with a 151km route from La Bourboule to Clermont-Ferrand. It is the first official mountain day of racing in the nine-day race, with six categorised climbs and 3,000m of elevation gain.

  • Côte de la Stele, 5.4km at 5%
  • Col de la Croix Saint-Robert, 5.2km at 6.4%
  • Col de la Croix Morand, 6.8km at 5%
  • Côte de Murol, 3.3km at 5.3%
  • Côte de Rouillas, 2.3km at 6.1%
  • Côte de Charade, 6km at 5.9%

The final day of racing will begin in Clermont-Ferrand and take the peloton on a 170km GC battle over eight climbs and 3,800m of elevation gain to the summit of the Puy de Dôme, where the overall winner will be crowned.

  • Côte de Ternant, 5.1km at 6.3%
  • Côte de L'étang des Ouches, 4.7km at 5.1%
  • Côte des Fades, 4.2km at 4.6%
  • Côte du Bouchet, 1.9km at 7%
  • Côte de Boisse, 1.3km at 7.3%
  • Côte de Saint-Jacques-d'Ambur, 2.6km at 5.9%
  • Côte de La Mouteyre, 5.3km at 6.2%
  • Puy de Dôme, 11.3km at 7.8%

items.title: Here is the new Tour de France yellow jersey – Castelli reveals leaders' jerseys for next year's races
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Both races are among the host of events for which the Italian company will provide leaders’ jerseys, the list also including the Vuelta a España, Vuelta Femenina, Paris-Nice and the Tour Auverge-Rhône Alpes.

However, the overall leader’s yellow jersey is the most iconic of all jerseys in our sport and it is the Tour de France which attracts most exposure for Castelli.

"For any cycling apparel brand, producing the Maillot Jaune represents the highest possible honor," said Castelli's Global Brand Manage, Steve Smith. "We wanted these jerseys to be truly special, which is why every micro-detail stems from our deep reverence for what they represent to the sport and the riders who earn them. Beyond pushing performance and aerodynamics, every single feature was crafted to honor that legacy.”

The colours of the jerseys are sacrosanct, and we’ll see no change from recent years, so there’s little room for radical new designs, but Castelli has added some neat little details to each of the jerseys which may make those riders wearing them feel a little more special - if that’s possible.

There’s Tour de France branding on each of the jerseys' zip pulls, which are hexagonal in a nod to France’s nickname, l’Hexagone, and when you open the zip of the yellow jersey, which Castelli say is more vibrant in colour, it reveals a red and blue trim which combines with the white zipper to form France’s flag.

While the red and white Castelli logo is visible on all the jerseys, the chance to incorporate it into the polka-dots of the mountain classification jersey was too good to miss, and adds a touch of class, as do the mountainous profiles on grip strips on the inside hem of the entire range.

The white, young rider’s jersey has undergone the most radical reform, with what they’re calling ultraviolet flashes added to the collar, sleeves and hemline to match the jersey’s new sponsor, Sanofi.

"This is not the first time Castelli and A.S.O. have joined forces around the Tour de France," Smith continued. "We previously produced the leaders' jerseys from 1989 to 1994, worn to historic victories by champions such as Greg LeMond and Miguel Indurain.

"Having supplied leader jerseys during that iconic era, returning to the Tour de France feels like a real homecoming. We are incredibly proud of our heritage in the race, but even more excited to shape its future by outfitting the next generation of champions with garments that push the boundaries of speed, comfort, and style."

Castelli will be providing jersey to a host of other ASO races, and while some, like Paris-Nice will be almost identical to those of the Tour, those of the Vuelta a España and Vuelta Femenina will be different and revealed at a later date.

items.title: Cannondale’s Connecticut HQ to close with the global headquarters moving to the Netherlands
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
American bike brand Cannondale is set to close down its Connecticut headquarters as part of a restructuring by its parent company, Pon Holdings and its US brands; the move is set to see multiple jobs lost.

For years, the company’s global headquarters has been in Wilton, Connecticut, but operations there will be wound down over the next eight months, with the company’s global base moving to Woudenberg, Netherlands, which currently serves as the European HQ.

Research and development, which is currently based in Freiburg, Germany, will continue.

The company’s North American HQ will consolidate with Pon’s other bike brands, Cervélo and Santa Cruz, moving to the West Coast. While it’s said each brand will retain its own identity, Pon says the move will "strengthen its North American operations and retailer support."

"This builds on two years of closer commercial collaboration between the brands to offer retailers greater choice.

"For retailers carrying more than one brand, this means a single point of contact and simpler ordering and support services.

"The aim is to make it easier for retailers to work with Cannondale and access more of the Pon. Bike portfolio," the company’s press release said.

Cannondale has been on the US bike scene since opening for business in Wilton, Connecticut, in 1971, and has established itself as one of the world’s largest bike manufacturers. Dutch multinational Pon Holdings acquired the brand from Dorel Sports in 2021.

The developments come just months after it was announced that Cannondale’s Dutch factory would close, with production moving to Lithuania and Germany and that their Mountain bike team, Cannondale Factory Racing, would close at the end of the year.

Despite its scale, the brand has always had a left-field feel, with its race winning, single-sided Lefty front suspension fork perhaps the company's most radical design. On the road, the brand currently supplies bikes to the EF Education-EasyPost WorldTour and EF Education-Oatly Women’s WorldTour teams.

"The entire office will be closed and almost all employees there will be impacted," said Cannondale’s Global VP, People, Maggie Lansdale, according to PinkBike.

"The first separations are expected to occur on December 21, 2026, and separations are expected to continue in phases through December 31, 2027. The closure and separations will be permanent."

items.title: Tour de France 2027 route unveiled with British start, 71km of time trials, and a brutal queen stage as highlights
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The route for the 2027 Tour de France has been unveiled, with a testing British Grand Départ, two individual time trials, and a brutal Pyrenean queen stage among the highlight obstacles that reigning champion Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and his challengers will have to face come July.

Race Director Christian Prudhomme revealed the route on Thursday at the Palais de Congrès in Paris, with the most ITT kilometres since 2012, when Bradley Wiggins took victory, totalling 71km across two key days against the clock.

Action kicks off from the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, on Friday, July 2, and 21 stages over 3,479km will stand in the way of whether or not Pogačar can win his fourth yellow jersey in a row and a record-breaking sixth overall crown in Paris.

The Pyrenees are set to star as the defining mountain range of the 114th Tour, arriving in the final week with a brutal duo of stages, including the hardest day on paper to the Col du Portet on stage 18, but the Alps and Massif Central will still play a major role in the race for the maillot jaune.

Even nine months ahead of the Scottish start, Pogačar is the benchmark that two-time Tour winner Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike), this year's runner-up Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), and rising French superstar Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) will all be chasing.

If he is to take a sixth overall victory, the Slovenian would move him ahead of Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, and Miguel Induráin for the all-time record of titles.

After likely battling out the race for the first yellow jersey on stage 1 in Carlisle, there are six probably flat stages in total where the sprinters and lead-out trains will want to come to the fore, with plenty on offer also for the rouleurs and Classics specialists as the race traverses south from the UK.

There would have been seven clear chances for the fast men, but the drama-producing Butte Montmartre climb has returned for a third year in a row in 2027 on the final day, making the run to the Champs-Élysées anything but a guarantee for those eyeing a sprint on stage 21 in Paris.

Organisers ASO want the GC race to be on for as long as possible, with a crescendo building towards the most difficult day on stage 18, where a back-loaded route will all but reach its denouement atop the Col du Portet summit finish, if someone isn't already out of sight.

Twenty years after the Tour started in London, and 13 years after mass crowds delighted the Tour in Yorkshire, the start in Great Britain is characterised by an opening flatter day, and two hilly stages to Liverpool and Cardiff, the second of which should bring the first major GC action.

in the tricky Welsh hills has five punchy climbs packed into the last 80km of a 223km day. The GC hopefuls will have to be at their best while the Classics specialists – including Pogačar – will surely be on all-out attack.

With more than 3,000m of elevation gain, it is a likely place for a signature Pogačar attack ahead of the first rest day, which is more of a travel day down to Normandy from the UK's south coast.

The first of two individual time trials comes on stage 7, where four-time ITT World Champion Evenepoel will be expected to take control over a flat 38km race against the clock in Chambord. The tension will be building over punchy finishes into the first few stages in France ahead of this important test.

Evenepoel has already won three time trials at the Tour, but without a major mountain stage in the first week, this could bring the Belgian his first stint in the yellow jersey, 51 years after the last Belgian winner of the Tour, Lucien Van Impe, unless Pogačar launched an early campaign of destruction on stages like the one to Cardiff.

If not, then he will have been keeping his powder dry for the Jura and the first trip up to the high mountains on stage 9, where a climb he has won before rears its head again: .

Pogačar took the second of his 26 Tour stage wins on the Grand Colombier on stage 15 of the 2020 race before winning his first yellow jersey, and now the 17.4-kilometre climb and its 7.1% average gradient represent the first opportunity to land a blow against your GC rivals. It arrives via the Col du Berthiand (6.3km at 7.5%), Côte de Neyrolles (3.6 at 7.7%), and Col de Richemond (7.7km at 6%), as the first of three mountain stages in a row.

As racing resumes after the first true rest day in Haute-Savoie, the host of the World Championships in 2027 will get a dress rehearsal for the rainbow jersey race on stage 10, a brutally difficult 171km route from Annecy to Sallanches.

The key climb of Worlds road races, the Côte de Domancy, will feature on the route as one of six tough climbs in the Alps. It's an ascent Vingegaard knows and loves, having demolished Pogačar there at the 2023 Tour en route to a second overall title.

But as we know, the Slovenian often likes to take revenge on the climbs where he has been burned in the past, and after missing out on defending his rainbow jersey this September, he will be hungry to make a statement.

The Tour will depart the Alps after just one more day of racing there, but it doesn't waste that opportunity, with the second hardest day on paper arriving on stage 11 to Les Saisies.

  • Time trials
    • Mountain stages
      • Summit finishes
        • Stage 9 to Grand Colombier
        • Stage 18 to Col du Portet

      More than 4,700m of elevation gain across four massive climbs feature, heading onto the Col de la Colombière (15.9km at 7%) straight out of neutral, and never really dropping in difficulty as it passes over the Col de la Croix Fry (7.2km at 5.5%), Col de la Forclaz de Queige (5.1km at 8.2%), Col du Pré (12.6km at 7.8%), and Montée de Bisanne (12.4km at 8.3%), before the final push to Les Saisies.

      After that complete reshuffle of the GC standings, the race settles into two sprint stages, but there won't be overly long for the riders to catch their breath, as they then reach the Massif Central, where 4,300 metres of elevation gain are tucked into a quite tough day to Mende on stage 14.

      The last time Mende appeared as a stage finish in 2022, there weren't major gaps between the GC favourites, as Michael Matthews won from the breakaway, but the approach to the finish in 2027 is over tougher terrain and steeper climbs, making the viciously steep Côte de la Croix Neuve (3km at 10.1%) more threatening than before.

      One of the big favourites will likely be in control by the time the second week reaches a close, but there can be no room for complacency heading into the final six-stage run towards Paris, with plenty of opportunities to lose and gain major time.

      The second individual time trial on stage 16 kicks this off, bringing the total kilometres against the clock to 71, returning the Tour to a stage closer to that of the Team Sky years, where Wiggins, Chris Froome and Geraint Thomas utilised the ITTs to their advantage, sometimes against the stronger climbers.

      This lands massively in favour of 2026 runner-up Evenepoel, who will likely have already won stage 7 and be looking to double up and further his chances of a repeat podium, or even higher. Staying with Pogačar atop Grand Colombier and in the Alps is far from a given, though, so for Evenepoel to even be within striking distance before stage 16 in Toulouse will be a tall order.

      What the 33km stage could do is potentially close the gap down before the Pyrenees, and this stage should also work in favour of home star Seixas, but Pogačar and Vingegaard are still not to be sniffed at – especially this far into a Grand Tour.

      What's certain is that the hardest stage of the race will come on stage 18: 174km, 5,400m of elevation gain, and four of the hardest climbs in the race and France packed into one day of Pyrenean fireworks, set to really separate the wheat from the chaff at the 144th Tour.

      Pogačar once again will return to favourable ground on a climb he has previously conquered, the Col du Portet (16km at 8.7%), which will serve as the summit finish and the Souvenir Henri Desgrange – the prize honouring the former director at the highest peak of the race.

      To get there, the GC favourites will have to survive the Col du Soulor (11.8km at 7.3%), Col du Tourmalet (19km at 7.4%), and Hourquette d'Ancizan (8.2km at 5.1%), with the Tourmalet's iconic slopes arriving with 70km still to go and offering up the chance for more daring, long range raids.

      Portet hasn't been seen in the Tour since 2021, when Pogačar defeated Vingegaard and Richard Carapaz en route to a dominant second yellow jersey title, but it will now headline the 2027 edition, as the likely penultimate major GC day.

      If yellow isn't all but decided by this point, which would be a major shock, then a second day in the Pyrenees will become the decider on stage 19, from Hasparren to Laruns, where the final climb to the Col de Marie Blanque (7.7km at 8.6%) presents the final chance for a long-range move, cresting 19km from the downhill run to the line.

      For now, Pogačar looks the most likely to be in yellow again at this point, but who knows what eight more months of development for Seixas and Evenepoel could look like – and Vingegaard isn't to be counted out with such brutal stages either.

      In theory, there could be a final day for major GC splits on the final day into Paris, with the triple ascent of the Côte de la Butte Montmartre again punctuating the final day, but GC times actually being taken and not neutralised as they have been the past two years looks unlikely.

      The Tour isn't just for climbers, even if yellow is the main prize, with plenty on offer over 12 potential non-GC days.

      With many of the best and most popular riders in the world being puncheurs or Classics specialists, it is in ASO's best interest to have days that suit the likes of Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike), and Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek) on the route.

      They've got them in abundance in 2027, especially in the first week, with stage 2 to Liverpool and stage 3 to Cardiff resembling profiles of Classics, with up-and-down tight roads in the UK set to bring the most explosive riders to the fore.

      Van der Poel and Van Aert have lit up hilly finishes in recent years, as have Pogačar and his newest lieutenant Isaac del Toro, so the GC riders likely won't be counted out of any of the short but steep uphill finales, such as on stage 4 to Cherbourg-en-Cotentin, the first day in France, or the following stage to Plumelec.

      • Punchy uphill finishes
        • Stage 4 to Cherbourg-en-Cotentin
      • Classics-style stages:
        • Sprint stages

          Stage 8 to Le Creusot also brings the same riders into play, but also represents a great opportunity for the breakaway, ahead of the first mountain stage. It's also the longest stage of the 2027 edition, with two tough climbs – the Col de la Croix de la Libération (4.6km at 5.3%) and Signal d'Uchon (5.7km at 5.7%) – preceding the uphill run to the line.

          Rodez to Albi at the close of the second week on stage 15 represents the likely final chance for the explosive Classics riders, until the last day in Paris, where Van der Poel's inspired win from a breakaway with Pogačar – just surviving ahead of the sprinters – should serve as inspiration for anyone with any punch left to get on the attack.

          At least six of the 12 non-GC days should be for the sprinters, including the opening day from Edinburgh to Carlisle, and flat finishes into Angers, Valence, Montpellier, Pau, and Libourne, with stage 21 to Paris also potentially going the way of the fast men depending on how it is raced.

          While the race for yellow has mostly been a dictatorship – or at most a duopoly if you go back from 2020 onwards – in recent years, sprinting has been more of a democracy, with the likes of Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep), Jasper Philipsen (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek), and Biniam Girmay (NSN) among those sharing the spoils in recent seasons.

          Merlier stands above as the best for the moment, but that balance of power changes quickly. However, all of the quick men will be thinking most about how they navigate the road from Edinburgh down to Carlisle, with a rare shot at yellow.
