items.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 route unveiled – Nine tough stages, a first-ever TTT, and a big Puy de Dôme finale
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The route for the 2027 Tour de France Femmes has been unveiled, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a traverse across northern and central France, and a challenging finale with back-to-back mountain stages in the Auvergne.

Kicking off on Friday, July 30, 2027, the sixth edition of the race will be nine stages long, the same as in 2026, with the final stage on Saturday, August 7.

Starting with three stages in Great Britain – two hilly stages around Manchester and the Pennines and then the race's first-ever team time trial in London – the race then returns to France via Calais.

The showpiece climb of the race will be the Puy de Dôme, a deeply historic Tour climb that returned to the route in 2023 after a long absence, and will be the climax of the race on stage 9.

Like last year, the course looks like one where practically every day could invoke GC action, with hills and tough roads from stage 1 and the TTT ensuring a GC hierarchy will be forming before the race even returns to France. From there, the journey across France is peppered with hills before the climax in the Massif Central.

2026 winner and world champion Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) will be seeking a third title, but will face tough competition from some familiar faces, including Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (soon-to-be Lidl-Trek), Marlen Reusser (Movistar) and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike), plus up-and-coming stars Paula Blasi (soon-to-be Movistar) and Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon-SRAM).

Where the race will be won

As we saw from this year's edition of the Tour de France Femmes, the yellow jersey isn't won on one or two big stages, it's a week-long battle with the favourites taking shots at each other wherever they can, including on the more innocuous stages. While there are still 'only' nine days of racing, and plenty of challenges on practically every day, we're expecting a similar pattern next August.

The final weekend with its back-to-back mountain stages will certainly be decisive, and will be where this race is officially won with the biggest time gaps here, but the GC action will have been brewing for several days already by the time the peloton hit the volcanic climbs.

Whilst the first two stages in the north feature plenty of spicy Pennine climbs, and the tension of the Grand Départ always throws up some twists, the flat finishes – and short length of stage 1, at only 87.5km – will likely mean we don't see huge gaps after those first stages. Some intention-laying attacks, sure, but the favourites should be on pretty even standings as the race heads to London.

The TTT around the capital will be the first guarantee of time gaps, then, with 18km of racing set around The Mall built by design to shake up the GC standings. Relatively short at 18km, the gaps again won't be huge, but they will be there. The team element is an interesting factor, though, as the specialists like Reusser and Vollering won't be able to just take chunks out of their rivals, they'll be limited by their teams, but on the other hand, riders like Ferrand-Prévot will be able to lean on their teammates more than they can in individual efforts. The yellow jersey won't be won or lost on the streets of London, but it will mean the riders return to France with an early idea of who is where on GC.

On returning to l'Hexagone, stage 4 won't offer up much of a break in hostilities, with the punchy finale into Calais sure to tempt the favourites into action, and the same could be said for stage 5 with its uphill finish into Manganville. The action here will mainly be feeling each other out, maybe grabbing a few seconds here or there rather than a race-winning gap, but with how close the favourites were matched this year, we know that every second counts.

This means that by the time we reach stages 7, 8 and 9 and their big climbing challenges, the GC tension will have been building for a good week, and we'll have a decent idea of who is sitting near the top of the standings, but there will still be a massive test to come.

It's hard to say which of the triple-header in the Massif Central will decide the winner of the Tour. Of course, a winner won't officially be crowned until the riders cross the line on stage 9 atop the Puy de Dôme, but could someone take enough time on stage 7 or 8 to put themselves well in the lead already? It's very possible.

The first summit finish of the race comes on stage 7, which is relatively late, atop La Loge des Gardes, a wooded ski station climb that's featured in Paris-Nice in recent years. The 6.7km climb is preceded by 30km of gradual, uncategorised climbing, which will sap the legs and could make it harder than its profile suggests, with big time gaps possible here. No one wants to leave it late, but equally, no one wants to play all their cards too early.

Stage 8 ramps up a level with no fewer than six climbs and 3,000m of elevation with a stage that could really rip the race apart on some of the hardest climbs in the Massif Central, but even after that, the Puy de Dôme will still be looming. A rider would have to have probably more than three minutes of a lead to feel comfortable going into stage 9.

Not only is the final stage packed full of climbing with a mountaintop finish atop the volcano, but it's long, too, at 170km. It's easy to imagine a scenario where a rider comes into this stage in yellow with a solid lead, but unless that lead is really huge, all will still be to play for on the 11.3km ascent up the Puy de Dôme. It's a lonely, testing climb, where gaps can open up quickly, and a final-day raid is far from impossible.

Whilst previous editions of the Tour haven't concluded on the showpiece climb – there's often been one last day to shake things out – 2027 will do just that, so expect everyone to throw absolutely everything at stage 9. And that could have some dramatic results.

As we saw in this year's Tour de France Femmes, opportunities for riders not aiming at the GC can be hard to come by. In 2026, practically every stage except the pan-flat openers ended up a GC race of some sorts, with the relatively short length of the women's race meaning the favourites wanted to take every opportunity they could to take time and shake up the standings.

In 2027, a similar story is expected. The backloading of the truly big climbs could swing the earlier stages slightly more in favour of the non-GC riders, but if history has told us anything about this race, it's that the favourites will go to battle as early as they can.

Stages 1 and 2, with their flat, city-centre finishes, look primed for sprints of some sort, but the pure sprinters will probably be looking on with a hint of dismay, because there are some truly tough Pennine hills on the routes which will put some of the weaker riders in trouble. 2026 green jersey Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) probably won't be particularly worried, though, and will see those opening days as another chance to add to her stage win haul and kick off her green jersey defense campaign.

Stage 4 looks primed for the puncheurs, though in this era, who are the true puncheurs? On these punchy finales – take the opening stage in Lausanne this year as an example – we often see all the GC riders getting involved, with Wiebes also more than capable of tackling all but the hardest climbs. The pure, non-GC puncheurs are probably the likes of Lotte Kopecky, Puck Pieterse and Kim Le Court-Pienaar, so this could be their rare chance at a stage win – if they can shake off, Wiebes, of course.

Stage 5 offers a similar opportunity, one should be for the puncheurs, but will likely see the GC contenders fighting for the win too.

The only true, true sprint stage of the race comes on stage 6, a pretty much pan-flat day form Orléans to Bourges that will surely finish in a big bunch sprint, with no late challenges to speak of.

Apart from that, riders who aren't the GC favourites or Lorena Wiebes may be looking at this course with a little bit of a disappointment. Breakaway stages are never guaranteed, and the backloading of the mountain stages means that they will almost certainly be won by GC riders, not breaks. So where can everyone else dream of taking a stage win? The first stages in France look to be the best chances, before the GC narrative takes over.

One quick look at the race map shows a glaringly obvious omission: no Alps or Pyrenees. This means the sixth edition of the race will be the first time since the inaugural event in 2022 that neither major mountain range is included on the Femmes route. Instead, limited by geography and time, the race will cut France down the middle with a trip into the Massif Central and the volcanic climbs of the Puy-de-Dôme department.

Of course, the Massif Central is a mountain range in its own right, with some seriously difficult climbs – the Puy de Dôme is no less challenging just because its not in the Alps or Pyrenees – but it's just that bit less well known than the two really big French mountain ranges. And whilst the Puy de Dôme is iconic in its way, it doesn't have the global recognition that a Mont Ventoux or Alpe d'Huez does.

The other missing discipline is an individual time trial. The London TTT means that the race against the clock is on the menu, but the team discipline is a highly different demand, and will provide very different results than an ITT would. 2026's time trial in Dijon – itself only the second time an ITT has featured on the Tour de France Femmes route – was a brilliant race that threw up lots of GC intrigue, so it's a shame not to see a repeat in 2027. Many will be pleased, not least the home favourite Ferrand-Prévot who is weak against the clock, but many will be disappointed too.

With the race still only nine stages, the Tour de France Femmes can't yet go everywhere and do everything, and this 2027 route is a reminder of that and the limitations facing the race in its current form – and perhaps a good argument for making this event longer. But make no mistake: this is a super tough route that will deliver another year of fantastic, challenging racing for the yellow jersey.

items.title: 'I turned down a much bigger contract so I could race where I wanted' – Paula Blasi officially signs for Movistar after drawn-out exit from UAE Team L'IMAD
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Reigning Vuelta Femenina champion Paula Blasi has signed for Movistar for 2027, and the next three seasons, the Spanish Women's WorldTour team confirmed on Wednesday.

The 23-year-old announced back in September that she would be leaving UAE Team L'IMAD a year earlier than contracted, and that she had signed for a new team in 2027, but while it was widely reported that it would be Movistar, that wasn't confirmed until now.

The Spanish team have reportedly paid a hefty fee to buy her out of her contract with the Emirati squad, and secure her future.

Scorching a rapid path to becoming one of the best riders in the world, Blasi took massive victories at the Vuelta and Amstel Gold Race in just her first full season as a pro this year, also finishing fifth overall on debut at the Tour de France Femmes, and taking top-five finishes at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, La Flèche Wallonne, and the Tour Down Under.

"I'm at a point in my sporting career where I needed to take a different step and look for a team that believed in me, supported my goals and was as ambitious as I am," said Blasi.

"I'll be able to grow, share leadership responsibilities and learn from Marlen [Reusser], which will be important for my development as an athlete. And on top of that, it's my home team. It makes me even prouder to wear the jersey."

Blasi's exit from UAE Team L'IMAD has been a long and complex one, with plenty of speculation and drama surrounding the move which is one of the most significant transfers in the women's peloton this year.

According to Spanish newspaper , while Blasi is set to earn around €600,000 a year, she turned down significantly more money at UAE so that she could ride for Movistar, with an €85,000 buy-out clause reportedly being paid so she could exit early.

also explained why there was such a delay despite signing her new deal before the Worlds in September. This was due to the wait for approval from the UCI, after the Spanish team's boss Unzué and her agent Alex Carera – who also represents Tadej Pogačar – convinced her that the project at Movistar was the right one, having already started to look elsewhere.

"I turned down a much bigger contract so I could race where I wanted," Blasi told . "It’s no secret that UAE is one of the teams with the most money. If you turn it down, you’re surely turning down one of the biggest offers you could receive.

"I want to be in line with what’s going on and earn what I think I’m worth. But for me, it was more important to think about my sporting future. I didn’t want to earn a huge amount for three years and end up hanging up my bike because I couldn’t take it anymore. My priority was to go somewhere where I can sleep peacefully and my only goal is to train."

A homegrown star joins Movistar

Movistar described the arrival of Blasi as a further strengthening of the team's "commitment to women's cycling and to building a project capable of uniting the present and the future," adding her talent to the likes of established leaders Marlen Reusser and Liane Lippert, and rising young stars like Cat Ferguson, Paula Ostiz, and Alejandra Neira.

"We're extremely excited to finally announce Paula's arrival to our team for the next three seasons," said team boss Sebastián Unzué.

"Her signing represents another step forward in quality, allowing us to compete for the most important races on the calendar. I want to thank Paula for her trust and for believing in this project. We can't wait to start working together. Welcome, Paula!"

Blasi only turned professional in May 2025, making a mid-season jump from UAE's development team up to the WorldTour squad, where she impressed immediately, winning a stage and the best young rider classification at the WorldTour-level Tour de Romandie, and finishing sixth at the Tour de l'Avenir – but he improvement in 2026 has been nothing short of remarkable.

Her victory at the Vuelta – a historic first for Spain in the women's race, and marking the arrival of a new superstar – stemmed from two stunning second-place finishes to Les Praeres and the iconic Alto de l'Angliru, landing her the red jersey ahead of Anna van der Breggen.

The hype and transfer rumours followed Blasi everywhere for the rest of the season, with the confirmation having to wait until October that it was Movistar who had secured the most sure-fire prospect in the women's peloton, who looks set to lead the ongoing and next generation of stars.

items.title: EF Education-EasyPost pick up another climber for 2027 after Carapaz departure
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Ivan Sosa will return to the WorldTour after two years away racing for the Kern Pharma team, as EF Education-EasyPost announced they have signed the Colombian for the 2027 season.

"I've heard great things about EF Education-EasyPost from riders on the team. They speak very highly of the team," Sosa said in the EF Education-EasyPost announcement.

"I think the team gave me the opportunity - and will continue to give me the opportunity - to come back and take that leap forward. And I believe that by working together with everyone who's part of the team, I know we're going to be able to achieve great things and we're going to have lots of happy moments - lots of victories that we'll experience along the way."

Sosa was one of several talented riders scouted from Colombia by former Androni Giocattoli manager Gianni Savio in 2017. After a successful two-year stint with the Italian outfit, Sosa signed with Ineos and spent three years with them before moving across to the Movistar Team. While Sosa has yet to win at the WorldTour level, he is a formidable climber and valuable domestique with victories in the Vuelta a Burgos and Tour de la Provence.

However, his results suffered as the years went on, but after undergoing iliac artery surgery in 2025, he found his way back to the top step of the podium in the Tour of Turkey, winning a stage and finishing second overall. Sosa then had a solid ride at the Vuelta a España, finishing in the top 10 on two stages after making the winning breakaway.

"Everything's just getting better and better. I'm growing more and more, and I feel better and better," Sosa said. "I'm really happy, really pleased, because I also had the chance to see how my body was holding up, and I realise that I'm fine now.

"It really motivates me to be able to rejoin the WorldTour and know that I'll have the team's support - everyone's support - and that we'll be able to improve and win races. That's what I want and what I think the team wants, too."

"Ivan is on his way to firing on all cylinders for the first time in a few years," Vaughters said. "He's going to be a huge help to our team when we're racing in the high mountains. He is savvy enough to get himself into a strong breakaway, and then he's strong enough to be able to make it to the finale.

"We saw him do that twice at the Vuelta a España. And after his recovery from iliac artery surgery, he has shown how motivated he is to race aggressively in search of wins. That's the kind of rider we look for."

The route presentation of the 2027 Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes will take place in Paris at 11am CET on Thursday, October 22, and you can watch it live with all the information following in our comprehensive guide.

The 2026 road cycling season is drawing to a close, but preparations for next year are already getting underway, with the unveiling of the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes routes a major event of the offseason.

There have been plenty of Tour de France route rumours circulating ahead of the presentation ceremony this week. British Grand Départs are already confirmed for both races, too.

The women's race looks set to then traverse across France, including a visit to the famous Puy de Dôme climb as a race centrepiece. The men's Tour looks set to feature the Grand Colombier and the Col du Tourmalet, with the famous final day Montmartre stage also set to be revisited.

The route presentation of the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes will be available to watch on several platforms across the world, with free coverage in some countries, so read on for all the details on how to watch the route presentation online, on TV, and from anywhere.

You can watch the Tour de France route presentation for free in many countries.

In Australia, coverage will be aired live on SBS, which requires registration but no payment to access.

items.title: 'Performances aren’t what you’d expect from a cyclist of his calibre' – Mystery surrounds Juan Ayuso’s 2026 race form
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After an excellent start to his time with Lidl-Trek, Juan Ayuso’s 2026 season didn’t go so well, with the 24-year-old failing to meet expectations; now his team are examining the rider’s data to ensure he is in top form for 2027.

After four years with UAE Team Emirates-XRG, Ayuso’s move to Lidl-Trek was one of the headlines of last year’s transfer season, and he was expected to challenge for the podium in Grand Tours. Though his overall victory at the Volta ao Algarve in February was a good start, his season has tailed off somewhat, with diminishing results.

Hopes were high when he took third overall at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (formerly Critérium du Daupiné) after finishing second on the two mountain stages, but seventh place at the Tour de France, behind his former UAE teammate, Tadej Pogačar, was a disappointment.

His lacklustre season has caused some head-scratching at Lidl-Trek, where they have been unable to pinpoint why Ayuso is unable to deliver the results they had expected.

"Something’s wrong, that’s clear; something’s not right, because what we’re seeing isn’t normal. The verifiable data we have from training doesn’t add up. The sessions have gone well; Juan has sacrificed a lot and invested a great deal to be in top form, with seasons at altitude and specific preparation for the World Championships, but then the race comes and things don’t go his way. His performances aren’t what you’d expect from a cyclist of his calibre.

"He’s sad, of course. He’s an ambitious and very hardworking guy. When we talk after the races, he asks me, 'Aritz, what do you think? What do you think is going on?’ And I tell him, 'I don’t know, Juan, we don’t have the answer.'"

"Right now, we’re in the analysis phase, trying to pinpoint the problem to understand what’s happening. And in that process, we’re looking at everything, from his health, with any potential medical issues, to his training data."

While Ayuso has been struggling, his team have been busy in the market, signing a raft of talent, including GC podium finisher Felix Gall, who joins from Decathlon-CMA CGM after a season where he finished second at the Giro d’Italia and third in the Vuelta a España.

Despite the Austrian’s arrival, there should be no change to what is expected from Ayuso.

"Juan’s goals for 2027 have to be the same as in 2026: to compete in a Grand Tour, one-day classics, and week-long races, which is what he’s done in his final years as a professional," Arberas continued.

"He’s a top rider, one of those from whom victories are expected, and he knows it; he’s fully aware of it."

Despite his experience and a palmarès which already includes 18 victories, Ayuso is still only 24 and, theoretically at least, he has plenty of time to mature into the Grand Tour challenger he was expected to. But with the constant influx of hungry, young talent into the sport, the pressure must surely be on.

items.title: Florian Lipowitz contemplates change of approach heading into second season as Red Bull leader alongside Remco Evenepoel
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
German stage-racing specialist Florian Lipowitz is eyeing a change in approach for the upcoming 2027 season, looking to improve his overall offering as a rider with more one-day Classics on his calendar.

Speaking on , Lipowitz already floated the idea and said: "I simply need to focus a bit more on one-day races and improve there,"which Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk has backed, saying it could help with his talents as a GC racer.

"I would even welcome that, because one-day races are ridden even harder than stage races," said Denk as reported by .

But he also asserted that "it has to be the right fit," for Lipowitz, one of the German squad's key leaders. "It's a balancing act."

A former Tour de France podium finisher in just his third year as a professional, Lipowitz entered 2026 with a schedule of only one-week stage races and the Tour de France – except for a team time trial dress rehearsal at the Trofeo Ses Salines – until he got injured.

While his level constantly improved from eighth in the Algarve to third in Catalunya, second in the Basque Country and Romandie, and finally to victory at the Tour of Slovenia, Lipowitz had his Tour abruptly ended during the stage 16 time trial. In one of the tightest corners, he crashed hard and broke his collarbone, abandoning the race having been sat fifth overall and in the race for the podium.

"I felt incredibly sorry for him at the time," said Denk, detailing how he then reassured Lipowitz, who started as co-leader alongside Remco Evenepoel at the Tour.

"We made it clear to him that he was on par with the very best in the first half of the season. He achieved podium finishes in Catalonia, the Basque Country, and Romandie. In addition, he won the Tour of Slovenia."

Lipowitz eventually made his return to racing at the Giro della Toscana, 50 days after his crash, and ended his season with four one-day race appearances, including at the World Championships in Montreal, finishing 47th.

Denk is eyeing up the brutally difficult Worlds road race in Haute-Savoie next year for Lipowitz, another reason for wanting to add more Classics to his calendar in preparation.

"The World Championships are incredibly tough with 5,000 metres of elevation gain, and that's exactly what Florian is suited to," said the team boss. "Therefore, it would be good if he did one or two one-day races beforehand."

He was due to race another one-day race in support of Evenepoel at Il Lombardia, but was forced to miss out due to illness.

Denk is certain the 26-year-old would have played a "good role" there, and said: "We missed him there – due to illness. I would have liked to have him with us." Evenepoel rode to fourth as Paul Seixas took solo victory.

Lipowitz and Evenepoel did butt heads momentarily during their Tour together as co-leaders, after the Belgian called out his teammate for not giving him a lead-out on stage 6, but the team and both riders squashed any potential issues the next morning. While their cooperation as co-leaders didn't get to play out fully after the German crashed out, Evenepoel's improvement in level to take second overall behind Pogačar adds to his standing as the team's main leader.

No decisions have been made yet over who will get leadership at which Grand Tour in 2027; they will only be confirmed on December 11 at the team's media day, but it would be unlikely to see Evenepoel not race the Tour again – even if he has said the door is not closed to potentially returning to the Giro d'Italia.

For Lipowitz, whose status is advanced as the German team's top home rider – an important figure for their German and Austrian title sponsors – his 2025 third place finish still holds him in good stead to potentially go back to the Tour, but Denk and his sporting management staff may want to spread their GC stars out, especially with Primož Roglič leaving the team.

When asked who would be riding where early into the off-season, Denk said: "That's a question that can be discussed. The outcome is still open," with the Tour route to be revealed on Thursday, October 22, and the Giro and Vuelta route to come out in November and December.

In 2026, Red Bull finished on the podium of all three Grand Tours: third at the Giro with Hindley, second at the Tour with Evenepoel, and second at the Vuelta with Roglič.

Denk's highlighted how "we've already won the Giro and know what that feels like. It definitely has its charm," suggesting he could be eyeing up sending one of his two main leaders to the Italian Grand Tour, though that spot could go to one of Hindley, or Italian riders Giulio Pellizzari and Lorenzo Finn, with Denk opting for Evenepoel and Lipowitz together at the Tour again.

items.title: 'It's a team I've always wanted to be part of' – Michael Valgren makes Netcompany Ineos switch for 2027
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos have announced the latest addition to their squad for the 2027 season, with Danish racer Michael Valgren joining on a two-year deal.

He joins after spending six years with EF Education-EasyPost and becomes Netcompany Ineos' ninth addition of the off-season.

"To finally have the opportunity to join Netcompany Ineos is a dream come true. It's a team I've always wanted to be part of, so in many ways, it feels like things have come full circle," Valgren said.

"I'm really looking forward to joining such a special organisation, where no stone is left unturned in the pursuit of performance. I believe the environment and resources here can help me find those extra few percent to raise my level and continue fighting for victories.

"Just as importantly, I want to use my experience to help bring the group together, support our collective efforts in races and guide the talented young riders coming through the team. That's something I'm really motivated by.

"I'm also really looking forward to working with Geraint Thomas, someone I've admired throughout my career. His dedication and work ethic have always been a source of inspiration for me, and I hope I can play my part in carrying on the legacy he's built within the team."

Valgren has been a solid Classics rider during his time in the professional peloton with Tinkoff-Saxo, Astana, Dimension Data, and EF. Alongside his two big WorldTour Classics victories are wins at the Coppa Sabatini and Giro della Toscana, as well as further podiums at Amstel, the Bretagne Classic, and at the 2021 Road World Championships in Leuven.

In recent years, Valgren has battled back from a career-threatening crash suffered in June 2022, which left him with a fractured pelvis, ruptured ACL, MCL and meniscus in his knee.

He returned to action the following April, under contract with EF's development team, before moving back up to the WorldTour squad in 2024. This season has represented a comeback of sorts to his previous top level, having scored a stage 5 breakaway victory at Tirreno-Adriatico in addition to that Giro stage win.

"I've known Michael personally for a long time, and I've always had a lot of respect for him, both as a rider and as a person. He's a great character who I know will fit really well into the team," said Netcompany Ineos director of racing, Geraint Thomas.

"He brings a huge amount of experience and has shown he's still racing at an incredibly high level, particularly after everything he's been through following his crash. To come back from that and be winning big races again says a lot about his character and determination.

"He'll bring real strength and experience to our Classics group, but just as importantly, he'll be a great addition to the team off the bike too. We're really looking forward to having him with us."

Valgren is the latest rider to join Netcompany Ineos as the squad gets overhauled for 2027. He joins James Shaw and Markel Beloki in switching over from EF, while other notable names to join the British team include Clément Champoussin, Harold Tejada (both from XDS-Astana), and highly-rated Spanish junior double world champion Benjamin Noval.

items.title: Fans forced to pay to attend Tour de France 2027 opening ceremony and teams presentation for the first time since 2014
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The teams presentation for next year’s Tour de France will happen in Edinburgh, but if you want to go along you’ll have to pay, with tickets going on sale this weekend.

The Tour de France returns to Britain in 2027 for the first time since 2014, with both the men’s and the women’s Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift getting underway in the country, and the men’s team presentation will take place on Wednesday, June 30, two days before racing gets underway.

The event will take place in the grounds of Edinburgh Castle and will be presented by the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, celebrating Scottish culture as well as showcasing the riders on stage in front of the public.

On a hill above the city, the location has limited access and ticketing is necessary, but the cost, starting at £27 (€32, US$36) per ticket, is not cheap, especially for a race which is otherwise free to attend.

While some Tour de France team presentations have been ticketed, especially when held in a location with limited capacity, they are generally free of charge. The most recent example of fans having to pay to witness the event was in 2014, when the race last started in Britain. Then, access to the First Direct Arena in Leeds cost upwards of £45.

"Featuring Highland dancers, massed pipes and drums, and new music created specially for the occasion, the ceremony will celebrate Scotland's culture and creativity while marking the start of an historic Grand Départ," the organisers' press release stated.

"While the opening ceremony and presentation of the riders take place on the Esplanade of Edinburgh Castle, the celebrations will extend beyond its walls, giving fans across Scotland’s capital the chance to see the riders en route to the Castle and join in the festivities ahead of the Grand Départ,

If you’ve signed up for the Grand Départ GB newsletter, you will have early access to tickets starting from midday on Friday, October 23, with members of British Cycling, Scottish Cycling and Beicio Cymru able to buy them 24 hours later.

If you’re a Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo customer you can purchase your tickets from midday on Monday, October 26, with general public sales beginning at the same time on Friday, October 30. Full details can be found here.

The race begins in Edinburgh on Friday, July 2, heading into England to finish in Carlisle. Stage 2 takes the riders from Keswick to Liverpool, with the third stage entirely in Wales, starting in Welshpool and finishing in Cardiff.

There will be a separate presentation event ahead of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, though details will be announced in the coming months.

items.title: Tofik Beshir out of ICU and responsive after severe training crash
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Beshir, 19, was training near his Lees-McRae College in North Carolina when the incident happened, and he was airlifted to hospital in Tennessee where he remained unconscious and in ICU with "injuries consistent with brain shear trauma".

He was later moved to a hospital in Washington D.C. to receive ongoing care.

His team and family have decided not to share many specific medical details about the extent of Beshir's injuries, but in the latest update, Hall confirmed that he has left the ICU.

"In the past few days, Tofik has been moved out of the ICU and he is responsive," he said. "This is incredible news for him and his progress, but he still has a long way to go."

"Your thoughts and your prayers, they're working, they are absolutely working, so please keep sending those his way, to his family and to our team," Hall said. "He has a long way to go, and we are still in need of that miracle. We believe more good things are coming, but he needs everyone to continue praying and thinking about him."

Born in Virginia to Ethiopian parents, Beshir is a freshman at Lees-McRae college and has been racing on the US cyclo-cross circuit since he was a junior.

He took his first elite victory last winter, and this year raced the USCX series with the CXD Trek Bikes team. He won five of the six races to secure the overall series title just a few days before his crash.

items.title: Cycling airbag system Aerobag named one of the best inventions of 2026
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
A new wearable airbag safety device for cyclists has made it onto magazine's list of best inventions in 2026.

Belgian company Aerobag's device is among 15 entries in the magazine's list under the 'sports & fitness' category, among a total of 300 inventions "making the world better, smarter, and more fun" this year, Time say.

Aerobag is a system fitted into the straps of bib shorts which, according to the company, "uses nine sensors scanning 200 times per second to monitor body dynamics and detect crash anomalies". The airbag "deploys in 100 milliseconds" when it's triggered before folding back into place, allowing the rider to continue racing afterwards.

The Aerobag team, headed by Bert Celis, spent six years developing the Aerobag. They began work on the device after Bjorg Lambrecht's death at the 2019 Tour de Pologne.

"You're sending athletes down the road at 60, 70, 90k an hour in lycra. And that was it. That was the catalyst. My mission, my absolute mission, is that you, as a rider, wake up at home. You don't wake up in the back of an ambulance."

It remains to be seen whether wearable airbags such as Aerobag will make it to professional cycling.

The brand is are already working with several kit manufacturers including Nalini, Nimbl, and MOA, with Picnic PostNL and Visma-Lease a Bike having already tested the device.

Meanwhile, back in February, the UCI launched a consultation on the use of wearable safety technology. The governing body invited 'expressions of interest' from relevant parties to form working groups.

"Already in contact with several players in the sector, the UCI now wishes to broaden the initiative to the greatest number possible of manufacturers and institutes working on the development of airbags and technical apparel for cyclists," the UCI stated at the time.

"The objectives of this initiative are as follows... Regarding airbag systems: to define a clear framework and appropriate standards to enable the development and integration of such devices into cycling (in competition and training); Regarding technical apparel: to study the integration of airbag solutions into clothing and to identify ways to further strengthen the protection offered by textiles."

items.title: Richard Carapaz departure was 'the simple option' to cut costs, says EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Carapaz has been the US team’s star rider over the past four seasons, finishing on the Giro d’Italia podium in 2025 and also in the top 10 of the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, while winning nine races including three Tour stages.

This year’s Tour was a standout, as he won two mountain stages and clinched the polka-dot jersey the team have coveted for so long, and he capped off his season with fourth place at the Vuelta.

However, despite that success and despite having another year left on his contract, Carapaz will move on in 2027, which is explained primarily by the team's ailing finances.

"It was a little bit of a sad situation where our economic resources were stretched to the point that we needed to make some hard decisions," Vaughters told .

Vaughters indicated that the team were facing budget cuts of around 15%, with the departure of Oatly – a title sponsor of the women’s WorldTour squad – a key reason, alongside soaring operational costs.

"When it comes down to like, 'Well, what are the cost centres that you can get rid of?' Well, there's not so many options, right? A very simple option would be to just let your most highly compensated rider leave."

As such, it would appear that Carapaz was not exactly poached by NSN Cycling.

"We willingly let Richie go. It was not forced," Vaughters said.

EF Education-EasyPost have been active in the transfer window but have focused on value for money, picking up the struggling former Giro d’Italia winner Tao Geoghegan Hart on a one-year deal, as well as the former junior world champion Emil Herzog.

items.title: 'She has the engine, and she has the instincts' - Bodine Vollering steps up to the WorldTour with EF Education-Oatly
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
Bodine Vollering is set to step up to the WorldTour with EF Education-Oatly starting in 2025. The Dutch rider aims to continue her development after spending two seasons with the ProTeam VolkerWessels Cycling Team.

“I talked with Esra. The way she spoke about the vision of the team, the way she selected this group of riders, what she’s trying to achieve with them is all to get the best possible results. It’s not just taking a rider and then replacing her after two years. The team has long-term goals, and how they approach everything is really nice. With these conversations, wow, it really woke something in me,” Vollering said.

“And then I see the videos on YouTube. I see how they incorporate fun and how they have a balance between fun and achieving results. I think it’s a really nice environment.”

Vollering said she connected with the EF Education-Oatly team at Classic Lorient Agglomération, where she applauded their strategy and teamwork during the one-day top-tier event.

“I raced Plouay, and I saw the girls from EF Education-Oatly,” she said. “They were controlling the peloton. I saw how strong they were and I thought, wow, because Plouay is a long race. They were in control all day. That’s really amazing, and to be part of such a team, such a community, is exciting.”

This year Vollering was sixth at Festival Elsy Jacobs, and she has finished in the top 10 at Tour de Feminin and Region Pays de la Loire Tour. General Manager Esra Tromp said the team is looking forward to supporting her development in cycling.

"She has the engine, and she has the instincts. She knows the sport inside and out. But she has never had the luxury of being able to dedicate herself completely to racing and training, nor has she had the full range of resources and support to see how far she can go. We can provide that,” Esra said.

Vollering outlined her early experiences with riding as a child with her family but says that she prioritised high school as she got older. She says that following her sister Demi Vollering's career through two overall victories at the Tour de France and a recent win at the World Championships has inspired her.

"I got into cycling, and I did some races, but then when I was in high school, I had a lot going on, so I didn’t race anymore," she said.

"Later, with my sister Demi [winner of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes and world championships], I watched her races, and it really started the fire within me. I wanted to get back on a bike. I wanted to race again. I wanted to see where I could get.”

During the last two seasons, Vollering has split her time between cycling and studying to become a tax lawyer. After completing her thesis, she will focus solely on racing.

“I came to law, and then with my background in high school, I ended up in tax law. That was before I knew I was going to be a cyclist. Now I only have my thesis left to do. It’s exciting because from next year on, for the first time I will be a real cyclist. I can focus on cycling all the way, instead of always having to be exhausted because I have to study, and that's mentally exhausting," she said.

She said that while she enjoys long climbs, she believes the punchy race parcours suit her ability better. Her main goal in her first season with EF Education-Oatly will be to settle in with the team and play a support role for her teammates.

“To be realistic, my main goal for next year is to work for my teammates, and see how I can help them and learn from them the best I can. I think that's really nice to do. My big dream for the future, I dream of the Tour de France. Every year when I watch it gives me goosebumps. I want to be there one day. And also the classics. Amstel Gold because it’s the one big race in the Netherlands,” she said.

items.title: 'I don't want to be just going through the motions' – Lachlan Morton in search of even more freedom as he departs EF Education to go it alone
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It was back in 2013 that Lachlan Morton, a young WorldTour professional with Garmin Sharp, set out on an adventure with his brother that spawned the Thereabouts series. That series set the Australian on a path that would eventually send him wildly deviating from the life as a professional cyclist he had once envisaged for himself and fully embracing the opportunity to run an alternate calendar at EF Pro Cycling.

Now, after eight years pushing the pedals in the pink kit of the team from the United States, the rider who has won Unbound 200, set a record time around Australia and captured the imagination with his Alt Tour of the Tour de France is branching out on his own. He confirmed his departure to earlier this month.

Morton's last race with the team was the brutally tough 61km Three Peaks Cyclo-cross in the United Kingdom – which he won – at the end of September and then he quickly set off on his final adventure with the squad. That was his effort to beat the 160-year-old 1,998-mile (3,217-kilometre) horseback record across the American West with his own set of steel steeds, and it was a feat he well and truly pulled off as he eclipsed the six-day 21 hours and 15 minute mark by 19 hours and 45 minutes.

It wasn't exactly a pre-mediated plan to deliver such a jam-packed final send-off to the EF colours,

"It just worked out like that," said Morton of piling the two very different efforts into a narrow window. "But I'm glad it did because it kind of felt like those two events sum up my time with the team pretty nicely.

"Combining a three-hour race with a week-long push, is like it's been in my time with the team. I've combined a lot of different disciplines and elements of racing, and I've always enjoyed that kind of challenge."

It also harked back to the time when Morton's adventures were his own, not under the guise of a team but in the case of the Thereabouts enterprises, a shared endeavour with his brother Angus.

It was important to Morton that he was there to capture this pivotal career moment too, in fact that was reason for the late-season position of the ride dubbed the 'Pony Express'. The timeline needed to be pushed a little later than originally envisaged because his filmmaker brother had welcomed a daughter into the world a couple of months ago, in what is proving to be an era of new beginnings for the siblings.

Early deviations – 'I'm sure that they were not stoked'

It's a little hard to imagine Morton as anything but the multidiscipline adventurer now, but there was a time when he couldn't even conceive of the path that he ended up following with EF Pro Cycling. After all, what was on show at the time he was starting out was a far narrower version of what you had to deliver to be able to ride your bike every day and call it a job.

"I was very much a road racer, and all my my goals were to succeed and win races and do as much as I could in the WorldTour, and then that sort of started to shift," Morton told . "The more I was exposed to it, I guess I started to gradually follow the other passions in cycling and that was sort of happening outside of racing.

"But I never dreamed that I'd be able to race and follow those kind of passions, simultaneously or under one banner. Initially, it was definitely just kind of like a hobby, it was not very closely in line with with what I was doing for a job. I didn't think that the kind of set-up I've had at EF would ever be something that that I could actually do."

It certainly wasn't the norm for a WorldTour professional to go and spend his off season riding 2,500km to Uluru and filming the adventure along the way. But back then, a young Morton didn't really care to do the expected, and that was probably a good thing.

"I was pretty stubborn, and I would just do the things I was going to do anyway," said Morton when asked what the Garmin Sharp team thought when he embarked on the first of three Thereabouts adventures in 2013, with the next two in the Colorado Rocky Mountains and Colombia in the following three years. "So I don't think I really took notice of what people thought, you know. I think the film led reassessing a little bit what I was doing racing."

"I think around that period of time, in my second year with the team, I wasn't racing particularly well, I wasn't particularly happy, and I think in that time I was definitely pretty self-absorbed," said a frank Morton, who isn't afraid to lean into a bit of typical Aussie self deprecation.

"So I don't think I really cared too much what anyone thought, just like a typical like 20-year-old, 21-year-old who is trying to work things out. So yeah, I actually haven't really thought about what they thought. I'm sure that they were not stoked. Maybe, I remember my coach wasn't super happy about it."

Fast forward a few years to the EF Pro Cycling team that formed out of the shell of that original squad, and there was a wholly different attitude. In 2019 Morton, after his sojourn with Jelly Belly and Dimension Data – decided to head back to a set up which was now far more enthused about embracing the unconventional.

It was, in fact, a move he made even though at that point he was quite content in the WorldTour.

"With Dimension Data, I found that as a professional. I was like, 'OK, I found a nice groove here where I can be happy in my life, training and doing this thing and accept the level that'll get me," said Morton.

But the lure of alternative plan was too hard to pass up.

"I remember speaking with some friends of mine at Rapha at the time, and they sort of mentioned the possibility of this idea," said Morton. "Initially, there wasn't any team really attached to it, and still I committed to doing it, which at the time felt sort of risky because it didn't really exist at that time, and cycling, I think, was even more traditional at that time.

"So there was a slight worry about if I was able to do this thing. And then if it doesn't work, if it could be hard to be taken seriously after that. I also didn't know physically, when I started to do longer distance stuff, how that would affect my ability to race. I don't think anyone really knew at that time, but it was just too good of an opportunity, and there were too many things that I realised that I wanted to do other than just road racing, so I was like, 'OK, let's go for it'."

All in on the alternative calendar

Initially while at EF Pro Cycling, Morton combined his alternative calendar with stints of racing with the WorldTour team "as needed". However, as time progressed and Covid came and went, dropping that made more and more sense, particularly with the build in level that meant ducking into the pro road peloton less than ideally prepared was a huge challenge.

"As a rider, I've never had biggest engine, so I need to show up really prepared generally, especially in in that kind of racing," said Morton, who didn't have the room for the type of preparation required given the alternate schedule commitments.

"It was very hard to do the job I needed to do at the race, but also mentally to just like show up and get your head kicked in. So yeah, it just no longer made sense to me to be doing that, especially when it's like there's 18-year-olds who are knocking on the door that deserved that spot more than I did."

By that time, however, there was no doubt of the value of the alternative calendar with the 'Alt Tour' in 2021 a validating experience that capture the public's imagination and showed that "if you do things a little bit outside the box, there's still space for it, it still exists alongside the traditional path," explained Morton.

That and his latest adventure, inspired by an affinity for the courage and tradition of the Pony Express riders that delivered mail through the harsh terrain, were two of the memorable moments he picked out from his time with the team when we spoke to him in the days following the conclusion of his last adventure under its umbrella.

"That was really, really satisfying, from the the group of people I had there and then the route itself, and then the way I was able to ride it. That was a dream one for me, and also to be so removed from cycling in a way, the route itself, it's not one that's been ridden a lot," said Morton.

"It was also cool to get to a point where you could say to the team, 'Hey, I want to do this', and there wasn't a huge amount of questioning about it. There was a trust."

That trust, and evident satisfaction that comes through from Morton when discussing his time with the team raises on big question. Why is he leaving?

"Above everything, I think it's just time is probably the biggest reason," said Morton. "I also don't want to be just going through the motions, knowing I can just do this thing that that works for everyone and just kind of be comfortable in doing that.

"The sport has changed very dramatically, I would say, in the last seven years that I've been with the team, and the the focus that is needed on performance I think is pretty drastic. I just don't see myself fitting in with that really anymore."

So where does he see himself fitting and what are his plans now?

"I think there's some even longer rides I would like to do, and being able to have complete flexibility in my calendar, there's space to be like, 'OK, yes I can go on a ride for like six weeks here' which I'm really excited for," he said.

"I'm also excited to have time to go to specific places and dive into the cycling culture that exists there and learn in a way. Without going into the specifics of routes and places, I think there's a lot of learning I know I'm going to have to do and I'm excited for that."

Still, many things will also be similar, as while Morton says he is well aware of the benefits of the support he gets from the squad, he has put together a good group to fill some of those gaps. Plus the plan is to continue on the path of chasing a mix of races – with Leadville among his goals – and challenges that motivate him. There will, however, perhaps be more of an emphasis on the travel and exploration side of riding, much like where it all began with Thereabouts.

"I've had a lot of a lot of freedom," said Morton of his time with EF. "There hasn't been a lot of compromise on what I would like to do but I just think I'm interested to see where I end up with it, and the things I can do without that kind of attachment and also without the safety net.

"As a 34-year-old man, that has grown up in teams since I was 18 years old, I think it's time for me to get out there by myself."

items.title: 'Maybe I'll take up gravel' - Still seeking a 2027 contract, Taco van der Hoorn weighs his future
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
After a season full of setbacks and his contract with Lotto-Intermarché coming to an end, Taco van der Hoorn is uncertain whether he will be in the pro peloton in 2027, according to .

The 32-year-old made his reputation as one of the most aggressive riders in the bunch, and his breakaways paid off with a Giro d'Italia stage win in 2021 and a handful of one-day race victories.

However, he was sidelined for most of two seasons after a crash in the 2023 Tour of Flanders left him with severe concussion symptoms. He made his return late in 2024, going on to win the Elfstedenrace, but his last two years have been riddled with illness and injury, which can make contract negotiations difficult.

"At the moment, I actually have no idea what I'm going to do next year," Van der Hoorn said. "There is still a possibility that I will stay with my current team, but it is also possible that I will have to leave. There is also contact with other teams, but that is far from concrete at the moment. So it could go in any direction. It is quite possible that I will still be riding in the WorldTour next year, but it is also possible that I won't be able to find a team at all."

Teams have already had to file their paperwork, including rider contracts to the UCI for the coming season, but there is still time for riders out of contract to find teams before January. Van der Hoorn says his chances of finding a team are fifty-fifty.

"It could just turn out the right way, but it could also just not ... There are still a lot of good riders available on the market for many teams. That makes it difficult. I would really like to continue, because I still enjoy training, racing, and professional life immensely. The difficult thing is that you don't have it entirely in your own hands."

A litany of physical problems, including knee surgery in February and then compensatory pain in the other knee, ruined his spring. Then, just as he was getting back to his top form, another setback hit.

"In Poland, I was really good again. I was part of breakaways and noticed that I was starting to ride at my old level again. That was a huge relief. I regained the confidence that I could still fight for a win this year. And then I crashed again."

His fall in the Renewi Tour left him with a broken hand and elbow, but he still geared up for a return in October, closing out his season at the Eneco Tour.

"It wasn't easy mentally to get myself there again," he said. "But I wanted to try one more time. Of course, I felt the urge to prove myself. I wanted to show that I am still good enough."

Van der Hoorn believes he still has more to give to the sport, like controlling breakaways for a team leader, mentoring young riders or even taking up a completely different sport.

"Suppose it doesn't work out to stay in the WorldTour or as a pro on the road at all, then I could also take up gravel. There are no concrete plans for that yet, but it is something I aspire to. I just really still enjoy cycling and have a competitive mindset. Moreover, I could combine that well with finishing my studies."

Van der Hoorn studied exercise science and is currently pursuing a degree in psychology.

"I think that with my studies and ten years of experience as a pro, I have quite a strong CV to get started somewhere in sports. For example, as a trainer or mentoring young riders. But I don't have any concrete plans for that yet. If I don't manage to find a contract, it could just as easily be that I take a year off and focus entirely on my studies. I wouldn't mind that at all.

"If it ultimately doesn't work out, then so be it. For now, I still hope that I can continue my career as a professional cyclist. I am open to any adventure that comes my way."

items.title: Belgian climber makes rare switch from Soudal-QuickStep to Lotto-Intermarché
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The 27-year-old has been with QuickStep since turning pro in 2021 and has three wins to his name – the 2021 GP Industria e Artigianato, a mountain stage of the 2023 Tour of Oman, and a stage of the 2024 Tour of Luxembourg.

This year, he finished seventh at Amstel Gold Race and was fifth from the break on stage 12 of the Vuelta a España. He's moving to Lotto, the team his father, Wim Vansevenant, rode for between 2003 and 2008.

"Lotto-Intermarché is a team with so much history. Over the years, so many talented riders and team leaders have come through its ranks. For me, that's the best proof of the quality of the work being done here," Vansevenant said.

"That's a team I want to be part of. I see my future here. I believe just as strongly in the team's character as I do in the project itself.

"It's not about being part of a huge organisation, but about that family atmosphere. I could already see during the season that there's a really good atmosphere within the team, and I know that's when I can get the very best out of myself."

Riders moving between the two biggest Belgian teams is a relatively rare sight. Pascal Eenkhorn went the other way last year, while Philippe Gilbert's 2019 switch to Lotto was the second-most recent transfer between the two. Looking back another three years, Nikolas Maes and Laurens De Plus went in opposite directions.

Vansevenant is the 10th rider on the incoming list for Lotto next year as their roster gets a major makeover.

French climber Guillaume Martin heads the additions, while Colombian sprinter Juan Sebastián Molano is also joining the team. Meanwhile, homegrown stars Arnaud De Lie and Lennert van Eetvelt move elsewhere.

Vansevenant said he's looking forward to a new challenge with Lotto, noting that he hopes to win a Grand Tour stage while also targeting the Classics.

"Having something new to prove is always a good thing in a career. I've been around for quite a while now.

"I still believe that winning a stage in a Grand Tour is within my capabilities," he said.

"And of course, the Ardennes Classics remain a major priority for me. The Amstel Gold Race, Liège-Bastogne-Liège… Along with the Tour of the Basque Country and other races at that level. Those are the races where I still want to achieve results.

"At the same time, after seven years at the highest level, I'm also more than happy to support the younger generation at Lotto-Intermarché. I know how to position myself in the peloton and how races unfold. I'm happy to pass on that knowledge. I think that's how we can make each other stronger."

Team CEO Jean-François Bourlart praised Vansevenant's offensive racing style, calling him an "important addition" to the squad and saying he can also help the team's younger climbers, such as Jarno Widar.

"With his attacking style of racing, Mauri is a perfect fit for our team. He will be an important addition to our roster, particularly in the Ardennes Classics. He has already proven his qualities in those races over the past few years," he said.

"We are convinced that he can take further steps and achieve strong results within our team."

"At the same time, he brings valuable experience to our young group of climbers. We don't just develop talented riders; we also surround them with experienced riders who can help them take the next step. Mauri will play an important role in that process."
